posts.title: How digital forensics changed modern investigations
posts.author: Cory
posts.excerpt: Digital evidence went from a niche hobby in the 1980s to a cornerstone of modern criminal investigations.
body: In 2004, the serial killer known as BTK sent a floppy disk to police in Kansas. Dennis Rader had killed ten people between 1974 and 1991. He believed the disk was untraceable. He was wrong. Digital forensics experts recovered deleted data from that disk. It led them directly to a computer at a local church, ending a decades-long mystery.

That case shows exactly how the investigative landscape shifted. For most of history, police work relied entirely on physical evidence. Blood, hair, tire marks, and witness statements built the timeline. Now, a massive share of the record sits inside phones, laptops, and the logs that devices keep automatically.

The term digital forensics was originally a synonym for computer forensics. It expanded to cover the recovery, investigation, examination, and analysis of material found in any device capable of storing digital data. The discipline has roots in the personal computing revolution of the late 1970s and early 1980s. It evolved in a haphazard manner during the 1990s. Today, it is a primary tool for establishing the facts of a case.
## From physical traces to digital records

Forensic science is the application of science principles and methods to validate decision-making related to criminal and civil law. The ancient world lacked standardized forensic practices. Criminal investigations relied heavily on forced confessions and witness testimony.

The first written account of using medicine and entomology to solve criminal cases came from China in 1248. Song Ci wrote a book translated as Washing Away of Wrongs. He described how to wash and examine a dead body to ascertain the reason for death. In one account, an investigator solved a murder by instructing suspects to bring their sickles to one location. Flies gathered on a single sickle, attracted by the smell of blood, and the owner confessed.

By the 20th century, physical forensics had matured. Edmond Locard formulated the basic principle of forensic science, stating that every contact leaves a trace. For decades, investigators looked for physical traces like fingerprints, bloodstains, and toolmarks. Now, the traces left behind are digital.
## The early days and the first laws

Prior to the 1970s, crimes involving computers were handled under existing laws. The first specific computer crimes were recognized in the 1978 Florida Computer Crimes Act. That legislation targeted the unauthorized modification or deletion of data on a computer system. Canada passed legislation in 1983, followed by the US Federal Computer Fraud and Abuse Act in 1986.

The growth in computer crime pushed law enforcement to establish specialized groups. In 1984, the FBI launched a Computer Analysis and Response Team. The British Metropolitan Police set up a computer crime department within their fraud squad the following year.

Many early members of these groups were computer hobbyists. They directed the field's initial research. One of the first publicized examples of digital forensics happened in 1986. Cliff Stoll pursued hacker Markus Hess using computer and network forensic techniques. Stoll was not a specialized examiner. Many early forensic examinations followed that exact profile.
## Building the tools

During the 1980s, very few specialized digital forensic tools existed. Investigators often performed live analysis on media. They examined computers from within the operating system using existing sysadmin tools to extract evidence. This practice carried the risk of modifying data on the disk. That led to claims of evidence tampering.

The need for dedicated software was recognized in 1989 at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center. This resulted in the creation of IMDUMP by Michael White. In 1990, Sydex developed SafeBack. These tools allowed examiners to create an exact sector-level duplicate of a piece of digital media.

Creating this forensic duplicate meant the original disk remained intact for verification. By the end of the 1990s, more advanced commercial tools like EnCase and FTK were developed. Analysts could examine copies of media without using any live forensics. Today, investigators often use a write blocking device to prevent any modification of the original. Both the acquired image and the original data are hashed using algorithms like SHA-1 or MD5. The values are compared to verify the copy is accurate.
## Proving intent and breaking alibis

Digital forensics does more than identify direct evidence. It can attribute actions to specific individuals and evaluate the source of a document. It is also used to prove intent, known in the legal system as mens rea. The internet history of convicted killer Neil Entwistle included references to a site discussing how to kill people.

In 2007, prosecutors used a spreadsheet recovered from the computer of Joseph Edward Duncan to show premeditation. This evidence helped secure the death penalty. Sharon Lopatka's killer was identified in 2006 after email messages detailing torture and death fantasies were found on her computer.

Digital records also confirm or refute statements. During the investigation into the Soham murders, the offender claimed an alibi. That alibi was disproved when mobile phone records showed the person he claimed to be with was out of town. SMS data from a mobile device also helped to exonerate Patrick Lumumba in the murder of Meredith Kercher.
## Tracking movement through networks and devices

Mobile devices and network traffic provide a different kind of record. Network forensics monitors and analyzes computer network traffic for information gathering or evidence collection. Traffic is usually intercepted at the packet level. Unlike other areas of digital forensics, network data is often volatile and rarely logged.

In 2000, the FBI lured computer hackers Aleksey Ivanov and Gorshkov to the United States for a fake job interview. By monitoring network traffic from the pair's computers, the FBI identified passwords. This allowed them to collect evidence directly from Russian-based computers.

Mobile devices provide location information through inbuilt GPS tracking or cell site logs. These logs track devices within their range. This specific information was used to track down the kidnappers of Thomas Onofri in 2006.
## The branches of digital forensics

Digital forensics is branched into various types depending on the devices and media. Computer forensics explains the current state of a digital artifact like a storage medium or electronic document. It covers computers, embedded systems, and static memory like USB pen drives.

Mobile device forensics focuses on the recovery of evidence from devices with inbuilt communication systems and proprietary storage mechanisms. Investigations usually focus on call data and communications rather than the in-depth recovery of deleted data.

Other branches include database forensics, which uses database contents and log files to build a timeline. Cloud forensics applies these principles to cloud computing environments, addressing challenges like multi-tenancy and jurisdictional issues. The National Institute of Standards and Technology published a guide outlining cloud forensic science challenges.
## Legal boundaries and ongoing challenges

The examination of digital media is covered by national and international legislation. In the United States, the Federal Rules of Evidence evaluate the admissibility of digital evidence. The US Electronic Communications Privacy Act places limitations on the ability of law enforcement to intercept and access evidence. It makes a distinction between stored communication, like email archives, and transmitted communication.

The admissibility of digital evidence relies heavily on the tools used to extract it. In the US, forensic tools are subjected to the Daubert standard. The judge is responsible for ensuring that the processes and software used were acceptable. In 2003, researcher Brian Carrier argued that the Daubert guidelines required the code of forensic tools to be published and peer-reviewed.

The field still faces unresolved issues. One major limitation is the use of encryption. This disrupts initial examination where evidence might be located using keywords. It is estimated that about 60 percent of cases involving encrypted devices go unprocessed because there is no way to access the potential evidence.

As of October 2026, the only framework that addresses the use of remote agents by forensic tools for distributed processing is one developed by Adams. The standards continue to evolve as devices grow larger and more complex. The digital record is now a permanent fixture of the justice system. Look at the data. Review the timelines. See where the evidence points.

posts.title: The Murdaugh Murders: From Conviction to a 2027 Retrial
posts.author: Cory
posts.excerpt: South Carolina's Supreme Court threw out Alex Murdaugh's murder convictions over jury interference. His retrial is set for April 2027 in Sumter County.
body: On June 7, 2021, the chief financial officer at Peters Murdaugh Parker Eltzroth & Detrick confronted attorney Alex Murdaugh about $792,000 in missing funds. That same night, at 10:06 p.m., Murdaugh called police from his cellphone to say he had found his 52-year-old wife, Maggie, and their 22-year-old son, Paul, shot dead near the dog kennels at their hunting lodge in Islandton, South Carolina.

The killings set off a chain of events that unraveled a legal dynasty. For 87 years, three successive generations of the Murdaugh family had served as the 14th Circuit Solicitor, controlling the local prosecutor's office in the South Carolina Lowcountry. Alex Murdaugh, a fourth-generation attorney, eventually stood trial for the murders of his wife and son, a case that local media called the "trial of the century."

The record shows years of financial crimes, a roadside shooting Murdaugh later said he arranged, and a murder trial that ended in conviction, only for the verdict to be thrown out in 2026 because of what a court clerk said to the jury. The State of South Carolina is now preparing to try the murder case again.
## The Night of the Killings

Alex Murdaugh called Maggie on June 7, 2021, and asked her to meet him at the family hunting lodge, known as Moselle, reportedly so they could travel together to see his terminally ill father, Randolph Murdaugh III. Maggie texted a friend that her husband sounded "fishy" and was "up to something." She parked her car and walked to the dog kennels, where she found Paul.

Paul had been under indictment at the time for boating under the influence causing death, following a February 2019 boat crash that killed 19-year-old Mallory Beach. He had pleaded not guilty. That night, both Maggie and Paul were shot multiple times, with different guns. The indictment later stated that Alex shot his wife with a rifle and his son with a shotgun.

Murdaugh told officers he was not at the scene that night, claiming he had visited his mother, who has dementia, and returned to find the bodies. Cellphone data, including a video Paul recorded at the kennels with his father's voice on it, placed Murdaugh at the scene before the killings.
## The Initial Investigation and the Roadside Shooting

In the months following the murders, the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division (SLED) regarded Murdaugh as a person of interest. During this time, the law firm PMPED discovered Murdaugh had misappropriated funds and forced his resignation on September 3, 2021. The next day, Murdaugh called 911 to report he had been shot in the head while changing a flat tire in Hampton County.

He was treated for a superficial gunshot wound. While in rehab for an opioid addiction, Murdaugh told investigators he had staged the roadside shooting in the hope of being killed, so his son could collect life insurance money. Court documents alleged that he hired a former client to shoot him, for a payout of about $10 million. Days after the shooting, the South Carolina Supreme Court suspended his law license.

In July 2022, a Colleton County grand jury indicted Murdaugh on two counts of murder and two counts of possession of a weapon during the commission of a violent crime. He pleaded not guilty and was denied bond.
## The 2023 Murder Trial

The trial began on January 25, 2023, overseen by Judge Clifton Newman. The prosecution, led by Creighton Waters, argued that Murdaugh's motive was the stress of his impending financial crimes being discovered. Judge Newman ruled that testimony about the financial crimes was admissible, allowing jurors to consider it as a possible motive.

The prosecution presented timeline data from cellphones and car telemetry, and highlighted a video taken by Paul at 8:44 p.m. at the kennels, in which a witness identified Murdaugh's voice. Murdaugh's defense team, Dick Harpootlian and Jim Griffin, criticized the crime scene investigation, noting it was spoiled by rain and that friends and family were allowed to walk through it.

Murdaugh took the stand on February 23, 2023. He denied shooting his wife and son but admitted to repeatedly lying to law enforcement about being at the kennels that night, attributing the lies to paranoid thinking from his opioid addiction. He also admitted to stealing from clients and asking a relative to shoot him. On March 2, 2023, after less than three hours of deliberation, the jury found Murdaugh guilty on all counts. He was sentenced to two consecutive life sentences without parole.
## Financial Crimes and Federal Sentencing

The murder case was only part of it. On May 24, 2023, a federal grand jury indicted him on 22 counts, including money laundering, wire fraud, and bank fraud. He pleaded guilty to 22 state charges in November 2023 and was sentenced to 27 years in prison.

On April 1, 2024, Murdaugh was sentenced in federal court to 40 years in prison for financial fraud, to run concurrently with his state sentences. He was also ordered to pay $8.7 million in reparations to his victims, which included the family of Gloria Satterfield, a longtime housekeeper for the family who died in February 2018 after what was described as a trip and fall accident at the Murdaugh home.
## Jury Tampering Allegations and the Clerk of Court

In September 2023, Murdaugh's defense team alleged jury tampering by Colleton County Clerk of Court Rebecca Hill, who had released a book about the case. The defense claimed Hill had inappropriate contact with jurors and requested a new trial. Hill resigned in 2024 amid a SLED investigation.

On May 14, 2025, Hill was charged with felonies including misconduct and perjury. In December 2025, she pleaded guilty to obstruction of justice, perjury and two counts of misconduct in office. She admitted to showing sealed court exhibits to the media, lying about it, and using her office to promote her book, and was sentenced to three years' probation. The judge said her sentence would have been much harsher if investigators had found that she tampered with the jury.
## The Conviction Overturned

On May 13, 2026, the South Carolina Supreme Court unanimously overturned Murdaugh's murder and weapon possession convictions, ordering a new trial. The court cited "shocking jury interference" by Hill, saying she used her status as "an officer of the court" to "essentially implore the jurors" to convict Murdaugh. The court wrote that her actions were a "breathtaking and disgraceful effort" to undermine the jury process.

In May 2026, Murdaugh filed a federal civil rights lawsuit against Hill seeking $600,000; a federal judge dismissed it in August 2026. The state attorney general, Alan Wilson, announced plans to retry the murder case.
## Where the Case Stands

As of September 2026, Alex Murdaugh remains in prison on his state and federal sentences for financial crimes, to which he pleaded guilty. He has denied killing Maggie and Paul from the start. With the 2023 verdict thrown out, the murder charges are pending again, and he is presumed innocent of them unless a new jury finds otherwise.

Judge Debra McCaslin set the retrial for April 5, 2027, at a status hearing in June. She then ruled that the retrial could not be held anywhere in the 14th Circuit, finding that Murdaugh could not get a fair and impartial trial in Colleton County, and on September 8 she ordered it moved to Sumter County, about 80 miles from the original trial in Walterboro. At the June hearing, defense attorney Jim Griffin said he wants the DNA under Maggie's fingernails analyzed by genetic genealogy, and that he was not sure how long that would take.
A new jury will hear the case from the beginning, and it will decide on what is put in front of it in Sumter County, not on the verdict of 2023.

posts.title: Why Some Cases Stay Cold for Decades
posts.author: Cory
posts.excerpt: More than 345,000 U.S. homicides since 1965 are unsolved. Memory, evidence, tunnel vision and cost explain why some cases stall for decades.
body: The Murder Accountability Project counts more than 345,000 Americans killed since 1965 in homicides that remain unsolved, and says at least 4,000 killers get away with murder every year. Each of those is a case where the investigation ran out of leads. A cold case is an unsolved crime that is no longer under active investigation but where new information could still surface. Most are murders and rapes, crimes that generally carry no statute of limitations, along with disappearances where the person has not been seen for years.

Why one case is solved in a week and another sits for forty years usually comes down to ordinary, practical problems: memories fade, evidence is lost or was never collected, investigators fix on the wrong person, and the tests that might help cost money.
## Time works against memory

Eyewitness memory is fallible, and it gets less reliable as months and years pass. Witnesses fill gaps without meaning to. Stress and trauma distort what people recall. Investigators talk about the first hours after a crime or disappearance as the most valuable, because evidence is fresh and memories have not yet been reshaped by news coverage and conversation.

The abduction of Jacob Wetterling shows how long a case can drift. On October 22, 1989, the 11-year-old was abducted while biking home from a convenience store with two other boys in St. Joseph, Minnesota. The FBI questioned a man named Danny Heinrich in December 1989 and released him for lack of evidence. The case stayed unsolved for nearly 27 years. In 2015, new testing of DNA from a 1989 assault on another boy, Jared Scheierl, matched Heinrich. A search of his home led to child pornography charges, and in September 2016, as part of a plea deal on one of those charges, he led investigators to Jacob's remains and admitted in federal court to abducting and killing him.
## Evidence and the tools to read it

Physical evidence does not wait. It degrades, gets misplaced, or was never collected to modern standards in the first place. Many cold cases predate the tools that now solve them. The FBI's DNA index, CODIS, began as a pilot program in 1990, and the national index did not go live until October 1998. The FBI's fingerprint system was replaced by the more accurate Next Generation Identification system in 2014.

Even good evidence is useless without something to compare it to. A DNA profile with no match in any database just sits in a box until the database grows or the method changes. The 1976 killing of Karen Klaas in Hermosa Beach, California, is an example. A familial search of the state DNA database in 2011 found nothing. A second search in 2016 matched a close male relative of Kenneth Eugene Troyer, and in January 2017 the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department named Troyer as her killer. He could never be charged. Police had shot and killed him in 1982.
## Tunnel vision

Investigations go wrong in human ways too. Detectives can settle early on a theory or a suspect and stop looking elsewhere. Researchers and courts call this tunnel vision. The cost is two-sided: the real offender is overlooked, and an innocent person can live under suspicion for years.

The Wetterling case had both. Heinrich was questioned within two months and let go. Meanwhile, in 2010, the Stearns County sheriff publicly identified Dan Rassier, a music teacher who lived near the abduction site, as a person of interest, and investigators dug up his farm. Rassier was never charged. After Heinrich's 2016 confession, the sheriff said it essentially cleared him.

Resources shape outcomes as well. High-profile cases draw detectives and money. A killing that never makes the news, handled by a short-staffed department juggling current cases, is at much greater risk of going cold.
## When attention does not help

The opposite problem exists too. Elizabeth Short, later called the Black Dahlia, was found murdered in the Leimert Park neighborhood of Los Angeles on January 15, 1947. A total of 750 investigators from the LAPD and other departments worked the case in its early stages, and police interviewed more than 150 men as possible suspects within weeks.

The press coverage was intense and at times obstructive. Reporters from the Los Angeles Examiner called Short's mother in Boston and told her that her daughter had won a beauty contest, to draw out personal details before telling her she had been killed. Detective Sergeant Finis Brown blamed the press for compromising the investigation with its probing and unverified reporting. Over the years more than 500 people have confessed to the killing, some of them born after it happened. It remains unsolved.
## How cold cases do get solved

Joe Kennedy, a former North Carolina police officer, retired NCIS special agent in charge and founder of the Carolinas Cold Case Coalition, told USA TODAY that the three most common ways cold cases are solved are physical evidence, witness testimony and confessions. Time, he said, can help as much as hurt. Marriages end, friendships fade, and witnesses who once stayed silent may finally talk. Kennedy said confessions play a larger role than many people realize, because many offenders end up telling someone.

The 1994 killing of Robin Warr Lawrence shows evidence and confession working together. Lawrence, 37, was stabbed to death in her Springfield, Virginia, home on November 20, 1994, while her 2-year-old daughter was in the house. Blood evidence from the scene sat unmatched for decades. In 2023, after Fairfax County cold case detectives sent the DNA to Parabon NanoLabs for genetic genealogy analysis, they identified Stephan Smerk, a former Army soldier living in New York. Within hours of giving a DNA sample, he went to a local police station and confessed. He told them he knew he was going to kill somebody that night but did not know who. Smerk pleaded guilty to first-degree murder in October 2024, and on March 7, 2025, he was sentenced to 70 years in prison.
## The cost of new science

Genetic genealogy has opened many old cases, but it is not cheap. Michael Coble, executive director of the Center for Human Identification at the University of North Texas Health Science Center, told USA TODAY that such investigations can cost $8,000 to $10,000, particularly when analysts must first separate a mixture of DNA profiles. For a small department, he said, the choice can come down to a new police cruiser or one case.

David Mittelman, chief executive of the Texas lab Othram, said government funding tends to follow DNA testing protocols that have been in use for years, while newer technology is not subsidized the same way. A federal bill named for Carla Walker, abducted from a Fort Worth bowling alley parking lot in 1974 and found dead three days later, whose case was solved with genetic genealogy nearly 50 years on, would let existing federal grant money pay for genetic genealogy and would require that work to follow Justice Department rules. It passed the Senate in June 2026. As of the most recent reporting found, it was waiting on the House.

For families, the wait has its own name. Psychologists call it ambiguous loss: grief without an ending. The cases that stay cold longest tend to be the ones where several of these problems stacked up at once, and the ones that finally break usually do so because one of them changed.

posts.title: Murders in Moscow: The Kohberger Plea and the Fight to Undo It
posts.author: Cory
posts.excerpt: Bryan Kohberger pleaded guilty in 2025 to avoid a death sentence. In July 2026 he asked to withdraw that plea. Here is where the case stands.
body: On July 2, 2025, in a courtroom in Boise, Judge Steven Hippler asked Bryan Kohberger, "Are you pleading guilty because you are guilty?" Kohberger said yes. On July 27, 2026, in a handwritten petition, he asked to take that plea back, writing that he is innocent and was talked into a false confession. This post follows the legal case from his arrest to that petition and where it stands now.

The background, briefly. Four University of Idaho students, Madison Mogen, Kaylee Goncalves, Xana Kernodle and Ethan Chapin, were stabbed to death in a rented house on King Road in Moscow, Idaho, on November 13, 2022. Kohberger, then a 28-year-old criminology doctoral student at Washington State University, was arrested at his parents' home in Pennsylvania on December 30, 2022. How investigators reached him, through a white Elantra, phone records and DNA on a knife sheath, is covered in our post How Investigators Tied Bryan Kohberger to the Moscow Murders.
## A Capital Case

Kohberger waived extradition and was flown to Idaho on January 4, 2023, where he was held without bail in the Latah County jail in Moscow. On May 17, 2023, a Latah County grand jury indicted him on four counts of first-degree murder and one count of felony burglary. The indictment replaced a preliminary hearing that had been set for late June. At his arraignment on May 22, he stood silent, and the judge entered not-guilty pleas for him.
On June 26, 2023, Latah County Prosecutor Bill Thompson filed notice that the state would seek the death penalty.
## Pretrial Fights and the Move to Boise

Kohberger's defense team, led by public defender Anne Taylor, challenged the case on several fronts. A central target was the DNA. The defense argued that the FBI's use of investigative genetic genealogy, which built a family tree from the DNA on the knife sheath, violated his rights. In October 2023, Latah County District Judge John Judge agreed to review the genealogy records privately and decide what the defense could see. In February 2025, Judge Hippler refused to suppress the DNA and data from Kohberger's online accounts, writing that "suppression is not warranted on any of these issues."

The defense also argued he could not get a fair trial in Latah County because of the coverage. On September 9, 2024, Judge Judge granted a change of venue, calling it the most difficult decision of his career, and left the choice of a new location to the Idaho Supreme Court. On September 12, the Supreme Court sent the case to Ada County, more than 300 miles south in Boise, and assigned it to Fourth District Judge Steven Hippler. Kohberger was booked into the Ada County jail on Sunday, September 15.
Hippler later moved the trial from June to August 2025. In his final schedule, jury selection was to begin August 4 and opening statements August 18.
## The Plea Agreement

The trial never started. On June 30, 2025, it became public that Kohberger had agreed to plead guilty to all five counts in exchange for prosecutors dropping the death penalty. The deal called for four consecutive life sentences without parole and required him to give up his right to appeal.

The families split over it. The Goncalves family said on Facebook that they were "beyond furious at the State of Idaho." The Mogen family, through attorney Leander James, said it supported the agreement "100%."

At the July 2 hearing, Kohberger admitted to the four killings for the first time. On the courthouse steps afterward, James read a statement for the Mogen family about turning from tragedy and the uncertainty of the legal process toward the future. "We have closure," it said.
## Sentencing

Sentencing took most of the day on July 23, 2025. Relatives and friends of the victims gave impact statements. When Hippler offered Kohberger the chance to speak, he said, "I respectfully decline." Hippler imposed four consecutive fixed life terms without parole for the murders and 10 years for the burglary, and called Kohberger a "faceless coward."

Hippler also fined him $50,000 on each of the five counts, $250,000 in all, and ordered a $5,000 civil penalty payable to each of the four families. Restitution was left open for 60 days. On November 13, 2025, the third anniversary of the killings, Hippler ruled on Kohberger's objection to part of it and ordered him to pay for urns for Goncalves and Mogen. Within a week of sentencing, Kohberger had been moved to the Idaho Maximum Security Institution in Kuna.
## The Petition

Because the plea deal waived his right to appeal, a petition for post-conviction relief is the only route left to challenge the conviction. Kohberger filed one in Ada County District Court on July 27, 2026. He wrote that he received ineffective assistance of counsel and that his plea was not knowing or voluntary because it was induced by unkept promises and by threats from his legal team. According to CNN, he also claimed his lawyers did not disclose or review exculpatory evidence with him and gave him a "gross misrepresentation" of what a life sentence and death row in Idaho would mean.

In a statement to The New York Times, he wrote: "My actual innocence is my truth, and the plea, hinged on by false promises and blatant disinformation, MUST be withdrawn." The office of Anne Taylor declined to comment. The Latah County Prosecutor's Office also declined, citing "pending litigation." Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador said his office "stands ready to do whatever is necessary to ensure justice is fully carried out."

The Goncalves family answered the same day on Facebook, calling Kohberger "the mosquito you just can't seem to swat." They pointed out that he had never before claimed to be uninformed or pressured, that he had told the judge he was guilty, and that they were confident he would get the death penalty if the case went to trial. On September 17, Kohberger's own family said it supports his petition because it wants "the complete and unvarnished truth" told.
## Where It Stands

In August, Deputy Latah County Prosecuting Attorney Keith Scholl asked the court to dismiss the petition quickly, arguing that it "fails to raise a genuine issue of material fact." Hippler set a schedule anyway. Kohberger's new lawyers, court-appointed attorney Greg Rauch of Moscow and New York lawyer Jason Goldman, have until November 13, 2026, to file an amended petition. Hippler wrote that "if an evidentiary hearing is granted, it shall be set to commence on June 17, 2027," with a status conference on June 3.

On August 27, 2026, Rauch filed a motion to disqualify Hippler. It argues that the judge's earlier rulings and his comments at sentencing, including that he could find nothing "good or intrinsically human" in Kohberger, could create the appearance that he has already made up his mind. Kohberger has also asked to move the post-conviction case out of Ada County. Separately, court documents unsealed in September show that shortly before the plea, his trial lawyers told Hippler they were having difficulty making sure he could rationally understand his situation, and asked for more time and an expert evaluation. Hippler denied that request.

A hearing on the disqualification motion is set for October 15, 2026. As of October 5, the court has not ruled on whether Hippler stays on the case or whether Kohberger can withdraw his plea. He remains in prison serving four life sentences. If he did win a trial, the death penalty could be back on the table.

posts.title: How the FBI's ViCAP Database Links Violent Crimes
posts.author: Cory
posts.excerpt: ViCAP, launched in 1985, lets police match violent crimes across jurisdictions. A 2024 federal audit found only 9 percent of agencies registered.
body: In 2015, ProPublica reported that only about 1,400 of the roughly 18,000 police agencies in the United States took part in the FBI's Violent Criminal Apprehension Program, known as ViCAP. In 2024, a Justice Department inspector general audit counted 1,674 registered agencies, about 9 percent of the total. That number is the most important thing to know about the system. It can only link the crimes police put into it.
ViCAP is the FBI's national database for connecting violent crimes across jurisdictions. Here is where it came from, what goes into it, and why it has never worked as well as its founders hoped.
## A detective's idea

The program grew out of one Los Angeles homicide detective's frustration. In the late 1950s, LAPD detective Pierce Brooks was working the murders of young women who worked as models. He suspected the killer had struck before. According to ProPublica, Brooks spent a year reading newspapers at a library looking for similar cases. The killings were tied to Harvey Glatman, who was later executed.

Brooks spent years pushing for a computer system that could run that search for every police department at once. In 1985, responding to a congressional mandate, the Justice Department established the FBI's National Center for the Analysis of Violent Crime, and the FBI created ViCAP inside it. ProPublica reported that the system went online on May 29, 1985. Brooks was its first director.

The problem it was built to solve was simple. A killer who crossed a county or state line could leave each local department holding one piece of a pattern that none of them could see. ViCAP was meant to put those pieces in one place.
## What goes into the database

ViCAP does not take every crime. Under the FBI's criteria, as listed in the inspector general's July 2024 audit, it accepts four kinds of cases. Homicides and attempted homicides that are apparently random, motiveless, or sexually oriented, or are known or suspected to be part of a series. Sexual assaults committed by a stranger, or known or suspected to be part of a series. Missing persons cases where the circumstances indicate a strong possibility of foul play and the victim is still missing. And unidentified human remains where the manner of death is known or suspected to be homicide.

What separates ViCAP from a DNA database like CODIS is the kind of information it holds. CODIS stores genetic profiles. ViCAP stores descriptions of what happened: the victim, the location, how the offender approached and controlled the victim, and what was done at the scene. The audit puts it directly: the program's success in linking crimes depends on the quantity and quality of the behavior-based information agencies enter.
Since the summer of 2008, the database has been available to law enforcement agencies through a secure internet connection, so a registered detective can search it directly.
## Who runs it

ViCAP sits inside one of the FBI's Behavioral Analysis Units, part of the Critical Incident Response Group, at Quantico, Virginia. It is staffed by crime analysts, each assigned a region of the country, and by contracted developers who maintain the system. Analysts review entries, search for possible links, and send their analysis to the agencies involved. They can also issue ViCAP Alerts asking other departments for information about a case. In 2015, ProPublica reported that the program ran on about $800,000 a year with a staff of 12 analysts.

The FBI's behavioral side also produced the working definition investigators use for serial murder. At a symposium the FBI hosted in San Antonio, Texas, from August 29 to September 2, 2005, experts agreed on this definition: the unlawful killing of two or more victims by the same offender or offenders in separate events. Many earlier definitions had required three victims. The FBI definition sets no minimum time between killings.
## Why participation matters

For most agencies, entering a case into ViCAP is voluntary, and for years few did. ProPublica's 2015 investigation found the database held about 89,000 cases after three decades and received reports on far less than 1 percent of the violent crimes committed each year. Detectives told the outlet that the entry process was cumbersome. The original form had 189 questions. It was later cut to 95.
Canada took a different approach. Police there are required to enter qualifying cases into a similar system, ViCLAS, and ProPublica reported that it held more than 500,000 case records.

Some states have since made entry mandatory. Texas did it in 2019 and Georgia in 2021, and the Justice Department's Sexual Assault Kit Initiative made ViCAP entry a condition of its grants. According to the inspector general, submissions rose from 463 in fiscal year 2018 to 13,750 in fiscal year 2023, an increase of almost 3,000 percent.
## The 2024 audit

That growth created a new problem. The inspector general found that ViCAP's technology, staffing, and funding had stayed essentially flat while submissions surged. The result was a backlog of almost 19,000 case entries waiting for quality-control review. From October 31, 2022, through September 30, 2023, ViCAP delayed or denied 101 of 232 eligible requests for analysis, more than 40 percent, because of analyst workload.

Participation was still thin. As of October 15, 2023, 1,674 agencies were registered users out of about 18,500 nationwide. The New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago police departments together entered 63 cases between fiscal years 2017 and 2020, far fewer than the murders and rapes they reported to the FBI in those years. Chicago entered none from fiscal 2021 through 2023. The audit found the FBI had no comprehensive strategy and no performance metrics for the program, and recommended that it evaluate what staff and money ViCAP actually needs.
## What it can do when it works

The audit's own example of success is Samuel Little, who confessed to murdering almost 100 people across 19 states between 1970 and 2005. According to the inspector general, ViCAP played an instrumental role in convicting him by identifying what his cases had in common.

That is the system at its best, and it explains the limits too. ViCAP is not a profiler with a hunch. It is a records system, and it is only as good as what goes into it. A case that never gets entered cannot be linked to anything.

posts.title: The Killing of JonBenét Ramsey: The Crime and the First Investigation
posts.author: Cory
posts.excerpt: How six-year-old JonBenét Ramsey was found in her Boulder home in 1996, and what investigators did in the first ten years.
body: The first officer to search the basement of the Ramsey house on the morning of December 26, 1996, came to a door held shut by a wooden latch at the top of the frame. He looked at it and walked away. That afternoon, six-year-old JonBenét Ramsey was found in a room behind that door.

This post covers the crime and the first ten years of the investigation, from the 911 call to a false confession in 2006. The DNA evidence, the grand jury vote and what Boulder police are doing now are in a separate post on why the case is still open. No one has ever been charged in JonBenét's death.
## The 911 Call and the Note

Patsy Ramsey called 911 at 5:52 a.m. on December 26 and reported her daughter missing from the family's home at 755 15th Street in Boulder, Colorado. She said she had found a handwritten ransom note on a staircase near the kitchen. The note was addressed to John Ramsey, demanded $118,000, said he would be contacted that morning with instructions, and warned him not to call the authorities.

The amount was nearly identical to a bonus John Ramsey had received from Access Graphics, the computer company he founded, and investigators looked at employees there who might have known the figure. At about 370 words spread over nearly three pages, the note was unusually long for a ransom demand. Investigators came to believe it had been written inside the house, with a pen and a notepad that came from the Ramsey home. A practice draft was also found.
## The First Hours

Two officers arrived within minutes. They searched the house and found no sign of forced entry. One of them, Officer Rick French, went to the basement and stopped at the latched door without opening it. He later explained that he was looking for the route a kidnapper had used to leave, and a door latched from the inside could not have been that route.

The rest of the house was never sealed off. Because police were treating the case as a kidnapping, JonBenét's bedroom was the only room cordoned off to protect evidence. Friends, victim advocates and the family's minister came to the house to support the Ramseys, and visitors picked up items and cleaned surfaces in the kitchen. Detective Linda Arndt arrived at about 8 a.m. to wait for the kidnapper's call. The call never came, and no one ever tried to collect the money.
## The Discovery

At about 1 p.m., Arndt asked John Ramsey and a family friend, Fleet White, to search the house for anything out of place. They started in the basement. John Ramsey opened the latched door and found his daughter in a room beyond it. Duct tape covered her mouth, a cord was tied around her wrists and neck, and a white blanket covered her body. He carried her upstairs.

Moving her disturbed the scene before forensic investigators could document it. The handling of those first hours has been criticized ever since: the house left open to visitors, the hours that passed before a thorough search, and evidence handled before it was recorded.
## The Autopsy

The death was ruled a homicide. The autopsy gave the cause as "asphyxia by strangulation associated with craniocerebral trauma." JonBenét had an 8.5-inch fracture on the right side of her skull. The cord around her neck had been made into a garrote using the broken handle of a paintbrush. Part of that brush was found in a tub of Patsy Ramsey's art supplies; the bottom third of it was never found despite extensive searching.

There were indications that she had also been sexually assaulted. No semen was found. The autopsy also recorded material that may have been pineapple, eaten a few hours before her death. Photographs taken in the house that day show a bowl of pineapple on the kitchen table. Neither John nor Patsy Ramsey said they remembered putting it there or giving her pineapple.
## Two Theories From the Start

Boulder police focused early on John and Patsy Ramsey. They saw no forced entry and believed the scene had been staged. Handwriting examiners ruled out John Ramsey as the author of the note but could not rule out Patsy. The Ramseys denied any involvement from the beginning, and in April 1997 they placed a newspaper advertisement offering a $100,000 reward.

Others saw an intruder. Lou Smit, a veteran Colorado homicide detective, came out of retirement in early 1997 to work the case for the Boulder County District Attorney's office. He pointed to a broken basement window, two windows left slightly open for Christmas-light cords, an unlocked door and an unidentified boot print in the room where JonBenét was found. His theory was that someone came in through the basement window and used a stun gun to subdue her.

Critics of that theory noted an intact cobweb in the broken window, undisturbed cobwebs on the steel grate over it, and untouched plants around the grate. Believing the Ramseys were innocent, Smit resigned from the investigation on September 20, 1998, five days after a grand jury was convened. He kept working the case on his own until his death in 2010.

That grand jury heard evidence for 13 months. In October 1999 District Attorney Alex Hunter announced that no charges would be filed, citing insufficient evidence. What the jurors had actually voted did not come out for years; the companion post covers it.
## A False Confession

Patsy Ramsey died of ovarian cancer in June 2006, at 49. Two months later, on August 16, 2006, John Mark Karr, a 41-year-old American schoolteacher, was arrested in Bangkok, Thailand. In emails to a journalism professor he had claimed that he killed JonBenét.
His claim did not hold up. On August 28, 2006, prosecutors dropped the case after DNA testing failed to place him at the crime scene. He was never charged in her death.
## Where the First Decade Left It

Ten years on, the record held a child found dead in her own house, a ransom note written on paper from that house, a broken window with a cobweb still in it, a man who confessed and did not match, and male DNA that had matched no one. Each theory of the case leans on some of those facts and has to account for the rest. No one has been charged.

posts.title: The First Fingerprint Convictions: Argentina, London, Chicago
posts.author: Cory
posts.excerpt: A bloody thumbprint in Argentina in 1892, a cash box in London in 1905 and a painted railing in Chicago in 1910 brought fingerprints into court.
body: In 1892, in the Argentine town of Necochea, police inspector Eduardo Alvarez removed a section of a door because it carried a bloody thumbprint. That print solved the murder of two children. It is considered the first homicide solved by fingerprint evidence.

Before fingerprints, police identified repeat offenders with anthropometry, a system of body measurements devised by Alphonse Bertillon in Paris and first put to use in 1882. Over the next three decades, a handful of cases on three continents replaced it. Here is how the first ones happened, and what later research said about the method they established.

Using finger marks as a signature was not new. The National Institute of Justice's Fingerprint Sourcebook says friction ridge impressions were used as proof of identity in China perhaps as early as 300 B.C. and in Japan as early as A.D. 702. What was new in the late 1800s was the idea that a mark left at a crime scene could identify one person. In 1858, William Herschel, a British administrator in Bengal, had a contractor put his handprint on a contract, and he went on to use prints to prevent fraud. In 1880, Henry Faulds, a Scottish medical missionary working in Japan, published an article in the journal Nature proposing that prints left at crime scenes could identify offenders. In 1892, Francis Galton published Finger Prints, the first book on the subject, establishing that ridge patterns were unique and persistent.
## Argentina, 1892

Juan Vucetich, who worked for the police in La Plata, began experimenting with fingerprints in 1891 after studying Galton's research, and he devised his own classification system. A year later his method got its first real test.

In June 1892, the two young children of Francisca Rojas, a six-year-old boy and a four-year-old girl, were found killed in their home in Necochea. Rojas had a wound to her throat. She accused a man named Velasquez, who she said was jealous because she would not marry him. According to the NIJ sourcebook, local authorities beat Velasquez trying to force a confession. He did not confess.

Inspector Alvarez, who had been trained by Vucetich, was brought in from La Plata. He found the bloody thumbprint on a door, removed that section of wood, and compared the print with Rojas's own thumbprints. They matched. Shown the match, she confessed. Argentina went on to become the first country to rely solely on fingerprints as a method of identification.
## India, 1897 and 1898

The British Empire moved next. In Bengal, Edward Henry, the inspector general of police, worked with Galton and two Indian police officers, Azizul Haque and Hem Chandra Bose, to build a classification system. In 1897 the government of India approved fingerprints as the sole means of identifying prisoners.

A year later, a Bengal court used the system in a killing. A tea garden manager was found with his throat cut and his safe rifled. A blood smudge on a calendar in his dispatch box matched the right thumb of Kangali Charan, a former servant. The court's assessors would not convict him of murder because no one had seen the killing, but he was convicted of stealing the manager's property. The NIJ sourcebook calls it the first case in which fingerprint evidence secured a conviction.
## London, 1905

England adopted the Henry system after a 1900 committee recommendation, and Scotland Yard's Fingerprint Bureau was established on July 1, 1901. The case that put the method in front of a murder jury began on Monday, March 27, 1905, at Chapman's Oil and Colour Shop at 34 Deptford High Street. William Jones arrived to find the shop closed. Inside, the manager, 71-year-old Thomas Farrow, was dead. His wife, Ann, 65, was alive but unconscious. Both had been beaten. Ann Farrow died on March 31 without regaining consciousness. The cash box was empty, and two masks made from stockings had been left behind.

On the inner tray of the cash box was a greasy thumbprint. Detective Inspector Charles Stockley Collins of the Fingerprint Bureau ruled out the Farrows and Sergeant Albert Atkinson, who had moved the box with his bare hands. The print matched nothing among the 80,000 to 90,000 sets on file.

Witnesses Henry Littlefield and Ellen Stanton identified Alfred Stratton as one of two men seen leaving the shop. His girlfriend, Annie Cromarty, told police he had gotten rid of his coat. Alfred was arrested on April 2 at the King of Prussia pub, and his brother Albert the next day. Collins matched Alfred's right thumb to the print on the cash box.

The trial opened at the Old Bailey on May 5, 1905. Prosecutor Richard Muir called more than 40 witnesses. Collins took the jury through the comparison. The NIJ sourcebook puts the number of matching characteristics at 11; other accounts say 12. The defense called Dr. John George Garson, who testified that the prints did not agree. On cross-examination, Muir produced two letters Garson had written, one to each side, offering his services. The judge, Mr. Justice Channell, called him "absolutely untrustworthy."

On May 6, after about two hours of deliberation, the jury convicted both brothers. They were hanged at Wandsworth Prison on May 23, 1905. It was the first murder trial in England in which fingerprints were used as evidence.
## Chicago, 1910

In the United States, Dr. Henry P. de Forest began fingerprinting New York civil service applicants in 1902, the first systematic use of fingerprints in the country. The first criminal conviction came eight years later. Just after 2 a.m. on September 19, 1910, Clarence Hiller woke to the screams of his wife and daughter at their home at 1837 West 104th Street in Chicago. He confronted an intruder, and the two men fell down the stairs. His daughter later recalled hearing three shots. Hiller died by his front door.

Police stopped Thomas Jennings about half a mile away. He had been paroled six weeks earlier and was wearing a torn, bloodied coat and carrying a revolver. At the house, investigators found fingerprints in fresh paint on a railing the intruder had used to climb through a window. They photographed the prints and cut off the railing.

Four experts testified that the prints were Jennings's, among them Mary Holland, described by the NIJ as the first American woman to teach fingerprinting. The defense questioned the new technique, and attorney W.G. Anderson challenged the experts to lift his own print from a sheet of paper he had touched. The print was clearly visible, and the demonstration backfired. The jury convicted Jennings, and he was sentenced to hang. The Decatur Herald called it "the first conviction on finger-printing evidence in the history of this country."

On December 21, 1911, the Illinois Supreme Court upheld the conviction in People v. Jennings. "This method of identification is in such general and common use that the courts cannot refuse to take judicial cognizance of it," the court wrote. Jennings was hanged at the Cook County Jail on February 16, 1912. Simon Cole, a historian of fingerprinting at the University of California, Irvine, has described Jennings as the earliest published American case discussing fingerprint evidence, which made it a precedent for the whole country.
## Not infallible

None of this made fingerprinting infallible, and the record since shows it. In 2004, the FBI wrongly matched a print from the Madrid train bombings to Brandon Mayfield, a lawyer in Oregon. An FBI examiner had called the match 100 percent certain, and the bureau later apologized. In 2009, a National Academy of Sciences report noted that not all fingerprint evidence is equally good, because its value depends on the quality of the latent print.

In 2016, the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology concluded that latent print analysis is a foundationally valid subjective method, but with a false positive rate that is substantial and likely higher than many jurors expect. In the two properly designed studies it reviewed, that rate could be as high as 1 error in 306 in an FBI study and 1 in 18 in a Miami-Dade study.

The method that convicted Rojas, the Strattons and Jennings works much the same way today. Examiners compare ridge patterns and details, and a person makes the call. The early courts accepted that judgment largely on trust. The modern question is different. It is not whether every finger is unique. It is how often examiners get the match right.

posts.title: What Reasonable Doubt Actually Means in a Courtroom
posts.author: Cory
posts.excerpt: The Constitution requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt but no set definition of it. Here is what the Supreme Court and jury instructions say.
body: The Constitution requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt in every criminal case. It does not say what those words mean. In Victor v. Nebraska in 1994, the Supreme Court held that "the Constitution does not require that any particular form of words be used in advising the jury of the government's burden of proof." So the phrase every juror hears is explained differently depending on the courtroom.

It is the highest standard of proof in American law. It does not require absolute certainty, and it is not met by a belief that the defendant probably did it. Here is where the standard comes from, how judges explain it, and how it played out in two very different trials.
## Where the rule comes from

The constitutional rule dates to In re Winship, decided March 31, 1970. A 12-year-old boy in New York had been charged with taking $112 from a woman's pocketbook. The Family Court judge acknowledged that the proof might not meet the reasonable-doubt standard and applied New York's lower preponderance standard instead. In an opinion by Justice William Brennan, the Supreme Court held that "the Due Process Clause protects the accused against conviction except upon proof beyond a reasonable doubt of every fact necessary to constitute the crime with which he is charged."

That made the standard a constitutional requirement in every criminal prosecution, state or federal. Civil cases use a lower bar, usually the preponderance of the evidence, which means more likely true than not.
## How judges explain it

Because no wording is required, jury instructions vary. One widely cited version is the Federal Judicial Center's pattern instruction, which Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg endorsed in a concurring opinion in Victor. It reads in part: "Proof beyond a reasonable doubt is proof that leaves you firmly convinced of the defendant's guilt. There are very few things in this world that we know with absolute certainty, and in criminal cases the law does not require proof that overcomes every possible doubt." If jurors think "there is a real possibility that he is not guilty," the instruction says, they must give the defendant the benefit of the doubt and find him not guilty.

Many other courts use a different formula: a reasonable doubt is the kind of doubt that would make a reasonable person hesitate to act. The Court in Victor accepted that formulation. Ginsburg called it unhelpful, because the most important decisions people make in their own lives usually involve accepting risk and uncertainty, which is not what jurors are asked to do.

There are limits on what a judge can say. In Cage v. Louisiana in 1990, the Court struck down an instruction that equated reasonable doubt with a "grave uncertainty" and an "actual substantial doubt" and asked for "moral certainty." As the Court explained in Victor, words like "substantial" and "grave" suggested that jurors needed a higher degree of doubt to acquit than the Constitution requires.
## Who carries the burden

The burden rests entirely on the prosecution, element by element. The defendant does not have to testify, call witnesses, or prove anything. If the state fails to prove even one element of the charge beyond a reasonable doubt, the verdict should be not guilty.

Conviction also takes all of the jurors. In Ramos v. Louisiana, decided April 20, 2020, the Supreme Court held that the Sixth Amendment requires a unanimous verdict to convict a defendant of a serious offense in state court, ending the 10-to-2 verdicts Louisiana and Oregon had allowed. One juror who is not firmly convinced can block a conviction. That alone is not an acquittal. A jury that cannot agree is a hung jury, and the prosecution can try the case again.
## Raising doubt: the Simpson DNA evidence

The 1995 murder trial of O.J. Simpson, who was charged in the killings of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ron Goldman, shows how a defense can attack strong-looking evidence without proving what happened instead. Over nine weeks of testimony, the prosecution presented 108 exhibits of DNA evidence, including 61 drops of blood. Robin Cotton, director of the Cellmark Diagnostics lab, testified that only 1 in 170 million people shared the genetic markers found in Simpson's blood and in a blood drop recovered near the bodies. She put the figure for blood on a sock from Simpson's bedroom, which matched Nicole Brown Simpson's type, at 1 in 9.7 billion.

The defense summed up its answer in three words: compromised, contaminated, corrupted. LAPD criminalist Dennis Fung acknowledged that blood evidence had been collected in plastic bags rather than the recommended paper bags and kept in a police van without refrigeration for up to seven hours. Defense expert John Gerdes testified that the LAPD crime lab had a substantial and chronic contamination problem. The defense also suggested that blood on the back gate of Nicole Brown Simpson's home contained EDTA, a preservative used in lab blood tubes, implying it had been planted. Roger Martz, an FBI chemist the defense called to support that theory, instead testified that the levels he found were consistent with unpreserved blood.

The defense did not have to prove contamination or planting. It only had to leave jurors unsure whether the evidence could be trusted. On October 3, 1995, the jury acquitted Simpson. In a separate civil case in 1997, decided under the lower preponderance standard, a jury found him liable for both deaths. The two verdicts are a clear illustration of how much the standard of proof matters.
## Meeting the standard: the Vallow Daybell trial

The other side of the burden is that a defense does not have to put on any case at all, and a jury can still convict. Lori Vallow Daybell went to trial in Boise, Idaho, in April 2023. She was charged with first-degree murder in the deaths of her children, Tylee Ryan, 16, and Joshua "JJ" Vallow, 7, and with conspiracy to commit murder in the death of Tammy Daybell, the first wife of her husband, Chad Daybell, along with grand theft.

Prosecutors called about 60 witnesses. The defense called none, and Vallow Daybell did not testify. Prosecutors argued she acted with Chad Daybell and with her brother, Alex Cox, and that the killings were tied to apocalyptic religious beliefs and to money, including the children's Social Security benefits. Cox died in December 2019 and was never charged.

The timeline was part of the state's case. Tylee and JJ were last seen in September 2019. Tammy Daybell died on October 19, 2019. Lori and Chad married in Hawaii on November 5, 2019, about two weeks later. The children's remains were found on Chad Daybell's property on June 9, 2020.

On May 12, 2023, the jury found Vallow Daybell guilty on all counts. On July 31, 2023, she was sentenced to three consecutive life terms without parole. Chad Daybell was tried separately, convicted on May 30, 2024, and sentenced to death on June 1, 2024. In 2025, juries in Arizona also convicted Lori Vallow Daybell of conspiring to murder her previous husband, Charles Vallow, and of conspiracy in the attempted murder of Brandon Boudreaux. She is appealing the Idaho convictions, arguing among other things that she was wrongly denied the lawyer of her choice and a speedy trial. The state says the trial judge made no reversible errors. As of October 2026, the Idaho Supreme Court has scheduled oral arguments for November 2, 2026.
## The question in the jury room

Strip away the formulas and the question each juror has to answer is the one the federal pattern instruction puts plainly: am I firmly convinced? A juror who thinks the defendant probably did it, but sees a real possibility that he did not, is told by the law to vote not guilty. The system accepts that some guilty people will go free as the price of not convicting innocent ones. Justice John Marshall Harlan said as much in his Winship concurrence, writing that it is far worse to convict an innocent person than to let a guilty one go free.

posts.title: How Wrongful Convictions Happen and How They Get Undone
posts.author: Cory
posts.excerpt: What DNA exonerations and the National Registry of Exonerations show about eyewitness errors, false confessions and evidence that was withheld.
body: Leonard Mack was convicted in 1976 of rape and weapons charges in Westchester County, New York, and served about seven and a half years in prison. On September 5, 2023, his conviction was vacated after new DNA testing produced a database hit to another man, who, according to the Innocence Project, then confessed. The Innocence Project says Mack's is the longest wrongful conviction to be overturned on new DNA evidence that it knows of: 47 years.

Mack's case had the most common ingredient in the DNA exoneration record, an eyewitness who identified the wrong man. Here is what the numbers show about how wrongful convictions happen, who works to undo them, and how long it takes.
## The Innocence Project

The Innocence Project was founded in 1992 by attorneys Barry Scheck and Peter Neufeld as part of a law clinic at the Benjamin N. Cardozo School of Law in New York. It started with cases where DNA testing could prove innocence and now also litigates cases built on other kinds of evidence. It says it has helped free more than 250 people.

No one knows how many innocent people are in prison. The Innocence Project cites studies estimating between 2.3 and 5 percent of U.S. prisoners. A 2014 study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences estimated that if everyone sentenced to death stayed under that sentence indefinitely, at least 4.1 percent would eventually be exonerated, and its authors called that a conservative estimate.
## What 375 DNA exonerations show

The Innocence Project tracked every DNA exoneration in the United States from the first one, in 1989, until the count reached 375 in 2020. Those 375 people served an average of 14 years. Twenty-one had served time on death row. Forty-four had pleaded guilty to crimes they did not commit.

The causes repeat. Eyewitness misidentification was involved in 69 percent of the 375 cases. Misapplied forensic science was involved in 43 percent and false confessions in 29 percent. In 42 percent of the misidentification cases, the witness had identified someone of a different race.
The race of the people convicted is part of the record too. Of the 375, 225, or 60 percent, were African American, and 29, or 8 percent, were Latino.
DNA can also point toward someone else. As of August 2018, the Innocence Project counted 180 DNA exonerations, about half, in which the actual perpetrator had been identified.
## The wider count

DNA cases are only part of the picture. The National Registry of Exonerations, now a project of the University of California, Irvine, counts exonerations based on any kind of new evidence. As of October 2026, its site lists 3,863 exonerations since 1989 and more than 36,191 years lost. Its annual report, published April 6, 2026, recorded 97 exonerations in 2025, the lowest yearly total in its annual reports since 2013. Official misconduct was present in at least 70 of them, and mistaken witness identification in 23 percent.
## Eyewitnesses, confessions and informants

Eyewitness error leads the DNA cases because a confident witness is persuasive and memory is not a recording. In Mack's case, the Innocence Project describes the identification procedures as highly suggestive. False confessions and jailhouse informants are the other recurring problems. Informants are often offered something in return for testimony, such as a lighter sentence, which gives them a reason to say what investigators want to hear.
## Evidence that was withheld

Government misconduct includes failing to turn over evidence favorable to the defense, which prosecutors are required to disclose. Michael Morton was convicted in Texas in 1987 of murdering his wife and spent nearly 25 years in prison before DNA testing cleared him. He was released on October 4, 2011, and officially exonerated on December 19, 2011. His trial prosecutor, Ken Anderson, faced proceedings over evidence that had not been disclosed. In November 2013, Anderson entered a plea to criminal contempt, agreed to serve a 10-day jail sentence, resigned as a district judge and permanently surrendered his law license.

Ryan Ferguson was convicted in 2005 in the 2001 killing of Kent Heitholt, a sports editor at the Columbia Daily Tribune in Missouri. Both witnesses against him later recanted. On November 5, 2013, the Missouri Court of Appeals vacated his conviction, ruling that prosecutors had failed to disclose evidence showing that a key witness had lied at trial. The state declined to retry him, and he was released that month. His lawyer was Kathleen Zellner.
## The Innocence Network

The New York organization is one member of the Innocence Network, a coalition of independent groups that provide free legal and investigative help to people trying to prove their innocence. The Indiana Innocence Project became the network's 74th member in September 2025. The network's members operate across the United States and in a dozen other countries, and say they have collectively exonerated more than 850 people since 2005.

Some exonerees go on to do the work themselves. Jarrett Adams was convicted of sexual assault in Wisconsin at 17 and sentenced to 28 years. With the Wisconsin Innocence Project's help, he won a unanimous reversal from the federal Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals on June 30, 2006, on the ground that his trial lawyer had been ineffective. The charges were dismissed in 2007. He graduated from Loyola University Chicago School of Law in 2015 and in 2016 became the first exoneree hired as a staff attorney by the Innocence Project.
## Decades lost

Glenn Ford, a Black man, was sentenced to death by an all-white jury in Shreveport, Louisiana, for the 1983 killing of a jeweler. His court-appointed lead lawyer had never tried a case to a jury. He spent about 30 years on death row at Angola before his release on March 10, 2014, after the state revealed it had information, never disclosed to the defense, that another man originally charged in the case had confessed.

Archie Williams was convicted in Louisiana in 1983 of attempted murder, aggravated rape and aggravated battery and sentenced to life without parole. DNA testing the Innocence Project won in 2007 did not clear him. A fingerprint did. In March 2019, unidentified prints from the victim's bedroom were run through the FBI's Next Generation Identification system, and examiners concluded some of them belonged to a man who had pleaded guilty to other sexual assaults in the same neighborhood and died in prison in 1996. He was never questioned about this attack. Williams's convictions were vacated on March 21, 2019, 36 years after his arrest.

Perry Lott was convicted in Oklahoma in 1988 of rape, burglary and other charges and sentenced to 350 years. DNA testing sought by the Innocence Project in 2017 found two male profiles, neither his. He was released in July 2018 after more than 30 years, under a deal that required him to drop his challenge, and on October 10, 2023, a judge vacated his convictions and dismissed the case. Anthony Wright was convicted in Philadelphia in 1993 of a 1991 rape and murder, and avoided a death sentence by a 7-to-5 jury vote. DNA testing pointed to another man, and in August 2016 a jury acquitted Wright at a retrial after he had served 25 years.

Several of these cases turned on evidence that had been sitting in a police file, a lab freezer or a fingerprint card for years. The record does not show that the system usually gets it wrong. It shows that when it does, the mistake is hard to find and slow to fix.

posts.title: How Familial DNA Searching Works, and Where It Is Allowed
posts.author: Cory
posts.excerpt: Familial searching looks for close relatives of an unknown offender in state DNA databases. How it works, cases it solved, and where it is legal.
body: On April 28, 2010, California's state DNA lab ran a crime scene profile from the Los Angeles serial killings known as the Grim Sleeper case through its offender database a second time. The first try, in November 2008, had found nothing. This time the profile came back close to that of a man convicted the year before on a felony weapons charge, close enough to suggest a parent and child. Police arrested his father, Lonnie David Franklin Jr., on July 7, 2010. In May 2016 a jury convicted Franklin of 10 murders.

That technique is familial DNA searching. The National Institute of Justice describes it as an additional search of a law enforcement DNA database, run after a routine search finds no match, to develop leads on close biological relatives of the person who left DNA at a crime scene. It rests on a simple fact: first-degree relatives, a parent, child or full sibling, share more of their DNA markers than unrelated people do.
## Not the same as genetic genealogy

Familial searching is often confused with investigative genetic genealogy, the method that identified the Golden State Killer. They are different tools. Familial searching uses the government's own databases of convicted offenders and, in some states, arrestees, and the standard forensic markers stored in them. Genetic genealogy uses consumer databases where people uploaded their own ancestry results, reads hundreds of thousands of markers, and can reach second and third cousins. Familial searching is limited to close relatives who are already in a state database.
## How a search runs

Arizona's state crime lab publishes a plain description of the process. Software compares the unknown profile against every offender and arrestee profile and ranks the people most likely to be close relatives. The lab then runs additional male-line Y-chromosome tests on the male candidates and full testing on any who remain, narrowing the list to a few names or to none. Arizona accepts only cases with a full DNA profile from an unknown male, an unsolved violent crime against a person, other leads exhausted, and a significant public safety concern.

A name from that process is not an arrest. Investigators still have to find the actual offender among the relative's family and get a direct DNA sample to compare. The Arizona lab put the nationwide success rate at 10 to 15 percent of searches as of March 2021.
## The Llandarcy murders

One of the earliest uses came from Wales, before most American states had any policy on it. On Saturday, July 14, 1973, 16-year-old Sandra Newton disappeared after a night out in Briton Ferry. She was found raped and strangled near Tonmawr. Two months later, on September 16, 16-year-olds Geraldine Hughes and Pauline Floyd were found raped and strangled in woodland at Llandarcy after accepting a lift home from Swansea. Witnesses described a white Austin 1100.

Detectives questioned thousands of owners of that model. One was Joseph Kappen. When police spoke to him, his Austin 1100 was on blocks with its wheels removed, and his wife gave him an alibi that later proved false. The investigation was scaled down in 1974.

In 1998 scientists recovered a DNA profile from the clothing of Hughes and Floyd, and in 2000 it was searched against the UK database without a match. A reinvestigation, Operation Magnum, narrowed thousands of names to a priority list of 500, with Kappen at number 200. When detectives went to his Port Talbot address in August 2001, they learned he had died of lung cancer in June 1990.

South Wales Police then looked for relatives of the killer in the database. Kappen's son Paul, a car thief whose DNA was already on file, came back with a distinctive similarity to the crime scene profile. Kappen's body was exhumed in 2002, and forensic testing matched him to the murders. Police named him as the killer. He was never charged or tried because he had been dead for 12 years.
## The first New York City case

On February 24, 1999, 13-year-old Minerliz Soriano was last seen walking home from school in the Pelham Parkway section of the Bronx. Four days later her body was found wrapped in a trash bag in a dumpster behind a video store in Co-op City. She had been sexually abused and killed by compression of her neck. Semen stains on her sweatshirt produced a DNA profile that matched no one.

New York adopted familial search regulations in October 2017. In April 2019 the NYPD and the Bronx District Attorney's Office applied for a familial search, and the state database returned a link to the late father of the eventual defendant. Several relatives were ruled out. Investigators then focused on Joseph Martinez, who had been 27 and living in Minerliz's building in 1999, and who was known as Jupiter Joe because he taught astronomy to children. Police covertly collected his DNA, and it matched the sweatshirt.

Martinez was arrested on November 29, 2021, and pleaded not guilty. On November 14, 2025, a Bronx jury convicted him of two counts of second-degree murder. On March 26, 2026, he was sentenced to 25 years to life. The Bronx District Attorney called it the first case in New York City solved with familial DNA.

The legal ground under that case shifted while it was pending. In 2022 a state appellate court struck down New York's familial search regulations, ruling that the agencies that wrote them had exceeded their authority. On October 24, 2023, the New York Court of Appeals reversed that decision and held that the state's forensic science commission did have the power to allow familial searches.
## A 1995 Brooklyn case

On August 2, 1995, a 36-year-old woman was forced at gunpoint onto the roof of a building on Pulaski Street in Bedford-Stuyvesant, raped and robbed of her jewelry. A rape kit was collected at Brooklyn Hospital, but the DNA matched no one. In June 2005, before the statute of limitations ran out, prosecutors indicted the unknown man by his DNA profile.

According to the Brooklyn District Attorney's office, advances in familial DNA technology produced a person of interest in the summer of 2026, and an abandonment sample confirmed his DNA matched the rape kit. On September 18, 2026, William Stephens, 54, of the Bronx, was arraigned on charges including first-degree rape and robbery, and bail was set at $250,000. He is presumed innocent, and his next court date was set for October 30, 2026.
## Where it is allowed

California became the first state to adopt a familial search program, in 2008. As of March 2021, according to the Arizona lab, 16 states had active programs: Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Kentucky, Louisiana, Michigan, Minnesota, New York, North Carolina, Ohio, South Dakota, Texas, Virginia, Wisconsin and Wyoming. Maryland and the District of Columbia ban familial searches of police databases. Montana since 2021 has required a warrant for familial or partial match searches.
## What the database can and cannot see

Familial searching can only find relatives of people the state has already collected DNA from. The FBI's CODIS program began as a pilot in 1990, and the national index did not go live until October 1998, so older cold cases rely on whoever has entered state databases since. Kappen was found because his son stole cars.

That same feature is the main objection to it. Critics, including the Legal Aid Society in New York, argue that because police databases over-represent people from heavily policed communities, familial searching puts their relatives under suspicion far more often than other families. Labs that run the searches, such as Arizona's, limit them to unsolved violent crimes where every other lead has been exhausted. Both points describe the same thing: the search is only as wide, and as narrow, as the database it runs against.
