posts.title: How Cold Case Units Decide Which Files to Reopen
posts.author: Cory
posts.excerpt: A cold case moves when a new lead exists: testable evidence, money for the lab, a database hit. The Sherri Rasmussen case shows how that works.
body: The National Institute of Justice defines a cold case as any case whose probative investigative leads have been exhausted, regardless of how much time has passed. Nothing in that definition is about age. A case can be cold after two years or still active after twenty. It moves again when a new lead exists, not because an anniversary arrives.

The backlog those units work from is large. In a 2019 article on cold case best practices, NIJ put the number of unresolved homicides in the United States from 1980 to 2016 at an estimated 242,000. It said roughly 40 percent of homicides go unsolved, and that the national homicide clearance rate fell from 78.3 percent in 1975 to 59.4 percent in 2016.
Reopening a case usually starts small. It is an inventory of what sits in evidence storage and a decision about what is worth sending back to the lab.
## Which files go to the top of the pile

No unit can work every unsolved case at once. The NIJ guidance says to start with the investigations that have the most apparent means of resolution, and to weigh database hits, how easily a case could be resolved, and community interest when choosing. It lists the usual reasons a case becomes workable again: advances in forensic technology, growth in DNA and other databases, changes in relationships over time, a fresh review that turns up something missed, and renewed public attention.

In practice that means a file with untested biological evidence still in storage tends to move ahead of a file where the evidence was lost or never collected. Samples once thought unusable have later produced DNA profiles. A swab the lab of 1995 could not read may be readable today.
## Paying for the lab

Funding decides which of those samples actually get tested. NIJ issued its first solicitation for a grant program called Solving Cold Cases with DNA in July 2004. In 2005 it awarded $14.2 million to 38 state and local agencies, and in 2007 more than $8 million to another 21. The money paid for personnel and overtime, laboratory equipment and supplies, investigative travel, training, and outsourcing samples to private DNA labs.
A small department with a handful of unsolved homicides usually cannot absorb that cost on its own. A grant can be the practical event that brings a stack of old files back to a working desk.
## The Rasmussen file goes cold

The murder of Sherri Rasmussen shows each of those conditions in one case. On February 24, 1986, Rasmussen, a nursing director, was found beaten and shot three times in the Van Nuys condominium she shared with her husband, John Ruetten. The Los Angeles Police Department treated it as a burglary gone wrong.

Detectives Lyle Mayer and Steve Hooks noticed things that did not fit, including a bite mark on Rasmussen's arm. Hooks found it unusual, reasoning that bites in a struggle are more often inflicted by women, while most burglars are men. The burglary theory stood anyway, and the investigation stalled within months.

Rasmussen's father, Nels, told police he suspected Stephanie Lazarus, an LAPD officer who had dated Ruetten before his marriage. Mayer told him there was nothing there. The case sat for more than two decades.
## A missing swab

In the late 1990s the LAPD set up a unit to go through evidence in unsolved cases and decide what might yield new leads through DNA testing. In 2004, criminalist Jennifer Francis turned to the swab taken from the bite mark. It was missing from the property log. It turned up only after a search of the coroner's freezers; samples that old had never been entered in the computer system.

Francis found no match in CODIS, the FBI's DNA index. But the saliva on the swab came from a woman, which undercut the burglary theory. When she asked the supervising detective whether the female officer had been looked at, he insisted it was a burglary. The result went back into the file.
## Fresh eyes

In March 2008, Van Nuys homicide detective Jim Nuttall found a box near his desk holding two old case files. One was Rasmussen's. He and his partner, Pete Barba, read the female DNA result and treated the case as a murder with a staged burglary.

The file supported that. Rasmussen's jewelry box sat in plain view, untouched. The condo was inside a gated complex. The front door had not been forced. A stack of stereo equipment at the foot of the stairs had a bloodstain shaped like a thumb but no print, suggesting gloves, and the blood was Rasmussen's, suggesting the equipment was stacked after the struggle.

The detectives built a list of female suspects and eliminated all but Lazarus, by then a detective in the department's art theft unit. Investigators collected a cup she threw away while off duty at a Costco in Simi Valley. DNA from it matched the bite mark.
## The arrest and the confession

In June 2009, Robbery-Homicide detectives Greg Stearns and Dan Jaramillo asked Lazarus to come to the jail at Parker Center to help with an art theft matter. After she checked her gun and sat down, they told her they wanted to talk about Rasmussen. She said she recalled little, then showed more knowledge of the case, then accused her colleagues of treating her as a suspect. Asked for a DNA sample, she said she needed to talk to someone and left the room. She was arrested outside it.

At trial in 2012, prosecutors argued her motive was jealousy over Ruetten's marriage. In March 2012 the jury convicted her of first-degree murder, and she was sentenced to 27 years to life. At a parole hearing in November 2023 she admitted the killing for the first time, and a commissioner found her suitable for release. The full parole board rescinded that decision on October 2, 2024, after Gov. Gavin Newsom raised concerns. At a new hearing on February 12, 2025, parole was denied. She is next eligible in 2028.
## What clearance numbers do and do not show

Clearance rates have recovered from their low. The FBI's estimate for 2022 was 52.3 percent, the lowest it had ever reported. It rose to 61.4 percent in 2024, and the Murder Accountability Project reported in August 2026 that FBI estimates put 2025 at 68.8 percent, the largest one-year improvement on record and the best rate in a quarter century.

One detail in how the FBI counts these matters for cold cases. Clearances are recorded in the year the case is cleared, and some of them pertain to offenses from earlier years. An arrest in 2026 for a 1985 killing counts toward 2026. A department that clears a batch of old cases can lift its current rate even while recent cases stay open, so the published number does not cleanly separate fresh work from cold case work.

Most reopened cases do not end in an arrest. A reopening is a set of conditions lining up: the evidence still exists, a method exists to read it, money exists to pay for the test, and a database turns the result into a name. In the Rasmussen case, the evidence and the method to read it were in place by 2004, and the result pointed to a woman. What was missing was someone willing to follow it, and that took four more years and a box left near a detective's desk.

posts.title: Why Eyewitness Testimony Is Less Reliable Than Jurors Think
posts.author: Cory
posts.excerpt: Eyewitness misidentification played a role in 69 percent of 375 DNA exonerations. Here is what memory research says about why.
body: On July 29, 1984, a man broke into Jennifer Thompson's apartment in Burlington, North Carolina, and sexually assaulted her. She identified Ronald Cotton in a photo lineup, again in a live lineup, and again in court. She was sincere, and she was wrong. In 1995, DNA testing excluded Cotton and matched another man, Bobbie Poole, who then pleaded guilty. Cotton had served more than 10 years in prison.

Cases like Cotton's are the most common pattern in the DNA exoneration record. The Innocence Project found eyewitness misidentification in 69 percent of the 375 DNA exonerations in the United States through 2020. Here is what memory research shows about why confident witnesses get it wrong, and what courts and police have changed.
## How the Cotton identification was built

The details of Thompson's identification show how a memory can firm up after the fact. According to the Innocence Project, when she first looked at the photo lineup she said "it is between number four and number five." After looking again, she chose number five, Cotton. After his arrest she picked him out of a live lineup. A second woman attacked in the same neighborhood that night viewed the same lineups and did not identify anyone. At Cotton's second trial in 1987, that woman did identify him, saying she had been too afraid to do so earlier. When Poole was brought into the courtroom outside the jury's presence, both women said he was not their attacker.
After Cotton's release, he and Thompson met and became friends. In 2009 they published a book together, Picking Cotton, and they have spoken widely about changing how police conduct identifications.
## Memory can be rewritten

Memory is not a recording. In a 1974 study, psychologists Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer showed students a film of a car accident and asked how fast the cars were going. The verb in the question changed the answer. Students asked how fast the cars were going when they "smashed" into each other estimated 40.8 miles per hour on average. Those asked about cars that "contacted" each other estimated 31.8.

In a second experiment, a week after watching a crash film, students were asked whether they had seen any broken glass. There was none in the film. Sixteen of the 50 who had been asked the "smashed" question said yes, compared with 7 of the 50 asked the "hit" question. One word in an earlier question had added a detail to what they remembered.
## Confidence grows after the fact

Witnesses often become more certain over time, not less. Law professor Brandon Garrett, writing in Judicature in 2020, noted that eyewitnesses in wrongful conviction cases often testified with complete certainty at trial after showing a lack of confidence when they first made an identification. By the time of trial, he writes, an eyewitness's artificially inflated confidence complicates the jury's job of judging credibility.

That is why research has shifted attention to the first identification. In 2014, the National Academy of Sciences published Identifying the Culprit, a report on eyewitness evidence. It concluded that science has provided an increasingly clear picture of the limits of human perception and memory that can lead to identification errors. It recommended standardized lineup procedures, recording the witness's confidence at the time of the identification, video recording the procedure, and better jury instructions and expert testimony about memory.

The report also called for double-blind lineups, run by an officer who does not know which person is the suspect, so the officer cannot signal the answer even by accident. Garrett describes blinding as central to the scientific method because it reduces the risk of unintentionally biasing the result.
## Faces of another race

People are generally less accurate at recognizing faces of a race other than their own. Researchers call it the own-race or cross-race effect. A 2001 meta-analysis by Christian Meissner and John Brigham, published in Psychology, Public Policy, and Law, found that own-race faces were more often correctly recognized and less often falsely identified than other-race faces. In the Innocence Project's DNA exonerations, 42 percent of the misidentification cases involved a cross-racial identification. In the Cotton case, Thompson is white and Cotton is Black.
## How courts have responded

For decades, the main federal test has come from Manson v. Brathwaite in 1977. It asks whether a police identification procedure was unnecessarily suggestive and, if so, whether the identification was still reliable under five factors. In 2011, the New Jersey Supreme Court, in State v. Henderson, went further and endorsed detailed jury instructions explaining how memory works. Garrett notes that later studies found such instructions made jurors more skeptical of eyewitnesses but did not make them better at telling accurate identifications from mistaken ones.
## When the first look fails

Even in a case where the right man was eventually identified, the first look can fail. On July 14, 1974, people at Lake Sammamish State Park in Washington saw a young man with his arm in a sling who introduced himself as Ted and asked for help with a sailboat near a tan or bronze Volkswagen Beetle. Yet the Lake Sammamish witness detectives considered most reliable failed to identify Ted Bundy from a photo lineup later that year.

In Utah, after Bundy's arrest in August 1975, Carol DaRonch picked him out of an October 1975 lineup as the man who had called himself Officer Roseland and tried to handcuff her. A judge convicted Bundy of kidnapping her in a 1976 bench trial. The same kind of evidence that failed in Washington held up in Utah.

An eyewitness who is certain is usually not lying. That is what makes misidentification so hard to catch. The witness believes it, the jury believes the witness, and the procedure that produced the certainty is often invisible by the time of trial. The reforms that hold up in the research all focus on the first identification: run blind, recorded, and taken down before anything else can shape it.

posts.title: Chain of Custody: When Evidence Handling Sinks a Case
posts.author: Cory
posts.excerpt: Chain of custody is the record of who handled evidence. Here is what the rules say about gaps, and when bad handling actually keeps evidence out.
body: In April 2017, after years of litigation, 21,587 drug cases in Massachusetts were set to be dismissed. The evidence in those cases had gone through the state's Hinton drug lab, where chemist Annie Dookhan had tampered with and fabricated test results. Dookhan was convicted in 2013. The drugs had been seized and tested, but nobody could trust the record of what had happened to them in the lab.

That is an extreme case, but it shows what the chain of custody protects. Evidence is only useful if the jury can trust that the item tested is the item collected, and that nothing changed along the way. Here is how that record works, how it gets challenged, and what courts actually do when it has gaps.
## What the chain records

The chain of custody is the chronological paper trail showing who collected, handled, transferred, analyzed and stored a piece of evidence, and when. It starts at the scene. Investigators photograph an item before moving it, record where it was found, package and seal it, and give it an identifying number. Each person who takes custody after that is recorded.

Take a hypothetical knife found at a homicide scene. An officer collects it and seals it in a container. A technician signs it out, takes it to the lab and lifts fingerprints. An evidence clerk then stores the knife and the lifted prints and logs everyone who checks them out. If any of those handoffs is missing from the record, the defense can ask who had the knife and what happened to it.

A properly marked evidence package shows the case number, the exhibit number, a description, where and when the item was collected, and the collector's name and signature, closed with a tamper-evident seal. A broken or undocumented seal is one of the first things a defense lawyer looks for.
## Why some evidence needs it more

Not every item needs a complete chain. A gun with a serial number, or an object with distinctive marks that a witness can recognize, can often be identified on sight. Federal Rule of Evidence 901 allows identification by an item's "appearance, contents, substance, internal patterns, or other distinctive characteristics."

Fungible evidence is different. A bag of white powder looks like any other bag of white powder, so the prosecution has to show that the substance the lab tested is the one taken from the defendant. That is why so many chain-of-custody fights happen in drug cases, and why a lab like Hinton can undermine thousands of them at once.

Biological evidence raises its own problems. It can degrade or be contaminated if it is packaged, stored or handled badly. In the 1995 O.J. Simpson murder trial, LAPD criminalist Dennis Fung acknowledged that blood evidence had been collected in plastic bags rather than the recommended paper bags and kept in a police van without refrigeration for up to seven hours. The defense built much of its case around how the evidence was handled, and the jury acquitted Simpson.
## What the law actually requires

In federal court, the governing rule is Federal Rule of Evidence 901, and most states have a similar rule. Before an item is admitted, the party offering it "must produce evidence sufficient to support a finding that the item is what the proponent claims it is." A witness who recognizes the item can do that. For fungible evidence, the chain of custody usually does it.

Here is the part television gets wrong. A gap in the chain does not automatically get evidence thrown out. In Melendez-Diaz v. Massachusetts, decided June 25, 2009, the Supreme Court noted that "gaps in the chain [of custody] normally go to the weight of the evidence rather than its admissibility." In most cases the judge admits the item, and the defense uses the gaps to argue to the jury that it should not be trusted.

The same footnote addressed who has to testify. It is not the case, the Court said, that everyone whose testimony may be relevant to the chain of custody must appear in person. The prosecution decides which links to prove, but whatever testimony it introduces must be given live if the defendant objects.

Exclusion happens when the problems are serious enough that the judge cannot find the item is what the prosecution says it is, such as a missing link at a critical point or signs of tampering. The defense usually raises that through an objection or a pretrial motion to exclude. A motion to suppress, strictly speaking, asks a court to exclude evidence on constitutional or statutory grounds, such as an unlawful search, rather than on authentication grounds.
## The defense's tools

Finding a chain problem takes records: evidence logs, property receipts, lab bench notes and quality-control files. Under Brady v. Maryland, decided in 1963, the prosecution's suppression of evidence favorable to the accused violates due process when the evidence is material to guilt or punishment. Records showing that lab work was unreliable can fall into that category.

Those challenges also depend on having a lawyer who will make them. Gideon v. Wainwright, decided March 18, 1963, held that the Sixth Amendment's guarantee of counsel applies to the states in felony cases, so a defendant who cannot afford a lawyer must be given one. Strickland v. Washington, decided May 14, 1984, set the test for when that lawyer's work is so poor it violates the right: performance that is deficient, and a reasonable probability that, without the errors, the result would have been different. A failure to investigate an obvious problem with key evidence can be the basis for such a claim.

The burden never shifts. The defense does not have to prove that evidence was tampered with. It only has to raise enough doubt about the evidence that the jury is not convinced beyond a reasonable doubt.

When crucial evidence is kept out, or when its reliability collapses the way it did at the Hinton lab, the prosecution may have no case left. More often, the chain holds well enough to get the evidence admitted, and the fight moves to how much weight the jury should give it.

posts.title: How Forensic Genetic Genealogy Works, and the Rules Around It
posts.author: Cory
posts.excerpt: How investigators turn crime scene DNA into a family tree, which databases they may search, and the rules written since the Golden State Killer arrest.
body: On April 24, 2018, investigators arrested Joseph James DeAngelo, a 72-year-old former police officer, at his home in Citrus Heights, California. His DNA was not in any police database. What investigators found instead were his distant relatives, people who had uploaded their own DNA results to a free genealogy website called GEDmatch. From those cousins, a genealogist built family trees until the branches pointed at one man. On June 29, 2020, DeAngelo pleaded guilty to 13 counts of first-degree murder and 13 counts of kidnapping.

The method is called forensic investigative genetic genealogy, often shortened to FIGG or IGG. This post covers how it works, which databases police are allowed to search, and the rules that were written after the DeAngelo arrest. A separate post on this site looks at the cases it has solved and the places it falls short.
## Why the police database came up empty

Standard forensic DNA work compares 13 to 20 short tandem repeat markers, or STRs, between a crime scene sample and samples on file, according to the Justice Department. Those profiles go into the FBI's Combined DNA Index System, CODIS. As of June 2026 the national index held about 20.3 million offender profiles, 6.4 million arrestee profiles and 1.5 million crime scene profiles. A search produces a lead only when the person who left the DNA is already in it.

That was the wall in the Golden State Killer case. DNA linked the East Area Rapist and Original Night Stalker crimes in 2001, but the profile matched no one in CODIS. The offender behind 13 murders, more than 50 rapes and over 100 burglaries across California between 1974 and 1986 stayed unnamed for another 17 years.
## A different kind of DNA profile

Genetic genealogy starts with a different test. A lab develops a SNP profile, short for single nucleotide polymorphism, from the crime scene sample. Consumer DNA tests read hundreds of thousands of these markers, far more than the STRs used in CODIS. That density is what lets software estimate how much DNA two people share, and so roughly how they are related.

Police cannot run that profile through 23andMe or AncestryDNA. 23andMe says it releases customer data only in response to a valid court order, subpoena or search warrant. What investigators can search are databases where people chose to upload their results and where the terms allow police use, chiefly GEDmatch and FamilyTreeDNA. Customers of the big testing companies can download their raw data and upload it there.
## Building the family tree

The database returns a list of people who share DNA with the unknown profile, ranked by how much they share. In most forensic cases the best matches are distant: second, third or fourth cousins. A genealogist then builds each match's family tree backward through public records such as birth and death certificates, census sheets, marriage records and obituaries.

The goal is to find where several matches' trees meet at a common ancestral couple. From that couple, the genealogist works forward through every descendant and narrows the list by age, sex and where each person lived when the crime happened. What comes out is a lead, not an identification.

The confirmation is old-fashioned. Investigators collect DNA the person has left behind and run a standard STR comparison against the crime scene profile. In DeAngelo's case, samples came from his car door handle and from a tissue in his trash, and both matched. The match that goes to court is that STR comparison, not the family tree.
## How far the method reaches

A 2018 study in Science led by Yaniv Erlich analyzed data from about 1.28 million people who had used consumer genetic tests. It estimated that about 60 percent of searches for Americans of European descent would turn up a third cousin or closer, enough in many cases to identify someone using a family tree plus age and location. The authors projected that a database covering about 2 percent of a population would put almost everyone in that population within reach.
That estimate was for one ancestry group. The method works only as well as the relatives who have uploaded, so its reach is not the same for every family or every community.
## The rules came after the arrests

GEDmatch's own terms changed first. In May 2019, after police in Utah used the site in an assault case that fell outside the limits it had published, GEDmatch set every existing profile to opt out of law enforcement matching. Since then, police see only users who have chosen to opt in. A forensic genomics company, Verogen, bought GEDmatch in December 2019 and said users would keep that choice. Qiagen bought Verogen in January 2023.

The Justice Department issued an interim policy that took effect on November 1, 2019. It covers federal agencies and any agency using Justice Department money for genetic genealogy. Under it, the technique is for unsolved violent crimes, meaning homicides and sex crimes, and for identifying human remains, and only after a CODIS search has found no match and reasonable leads have been pursued. Investigators may use only services that tell their users that police may search them.

States followed in 2021. Maryland and Montana passed the first laws restricting police searches of consumer genealogy databases. Maryland requires a judge's approval before a search, limits it to murder, rape, other felony sexual offenses and serious threats to public safety, and requires that CODIS and other reasonable leads be tried first. Montana requires a warrant. Utah passed its own limits in 2023, restricting searches to violent felonies and missing or unidentified people and adding requirements for prosecutor approval and warrants.
## The privacy question

The person a genetic genealogy search identifies usually never uploaded anything. Their cousins did. That is the core of the privacy debate. One person's decision to share a DNA file can expose dozens of relatives who never agreed to it, including people who become suspects and turn out to have nothing to do with the crime.

Courts have not settled how the Fourth Amendment applies. Prosecutors point to the third-party doctrine, the Supreme Court rule that people generally have no reasonable expectation of privacy in information they voluntarily hand to someone else. The Court has not ruled on genealogy databases, and in its 2018 Carpenter decision it declined to stretch that doctrine to cover cell phone location records.

Ownership matters too. 23andMe filed for bankruptcy in March 2025, and in June 2025 a court approved its sale for $305 million to TTAM Research Institute, a nonprofit formed by co-founder Anne Wojcicki. The buyer is obligated to honor 23andMe's existing privacy policies and user consents. The genetic data of millions of customers changed hands in a court-supervised sale.

Here is the short version of what happens when a police department announces that genetic genealogy found its suspect. A SNP profile was compared against people who opted in to police matching. A genealogist built family trees from public records. Then a conventional DNA test on something the suspect threw away did the confirming. Whether that trade between solved cases and family privacy is worth it is a question the law is still answering.

posts.title: The Killing of Delaware Trooper Ty Snook at the Wilmington DMV
posts.author: Cory
posts.excerpt: Cpl. Matthew "Ty" Snook was shot from behind at a Delaware DMV on Dec. 23, 2025. What the State Police found, and what has happened since.
body: Cpl. Matthew T. "Ty" Snook was at the welcome desk of a Delaware DMV office when a man who had just taken a queue ticket shot him from behind. It was about 1:59 p.m. on December 23, 2025, at the Karen L. Johnson Division of Motor Vehicles on Hessler Boulevard in New Castle, just outside Wilmington. Snook, a Delaware State Police Corporal Grade One working an overtime assignment, was 34. This post sets out what the State Police investigation found and what has followed.
## Who He Was

Snook was from Hockessin. He graduated from Saint Mark's High School and wrestled at the University of Maryland. He joined the Delaware State Police on March 6, 2015, as part of the 88th Recruit Class, and spent his whole career at Troop 6 in Prices Corner, working C-shift. At his funeral, his troop commander, Capt. Kerry Reinbold, said Snook had helped train more than 20 recruits since 2018. He is survived by his wife, Lauren, and their one-year-old daughter.
## What Happened Inside the DMV

The State Police published their findings on January 16, 2026. According to that release, Rahman Rose, 44, walked into the DMV at about 11:30 a.m., sat briefly in the driver services area and left without doing any business. He came back at about 1:56 p.m. and took a ticket at the welcome desk, where Snook and a DMV employee were stationed. The two men did not interact.

About three minutes later, police said, Rose came up behind the desk and fired several rounds over a glass partition from a handgun he had kept concealed. The release says Snook "valiantly and heroically shielded the DMV employee from harm before he was struck again by additional gunfire."

What followed, in the State Police account, points to who the target was. Rose "allowed and encouraged several customers to leave the building while he remained inside," then "appeared to wait for responding law enforcement." Investigators found that the only other shots he fired were at the officers who arrived. At about 2:07 p.m., a New Castle County police officer shot Rose through a window from outside the building. He was taken to a hospital, where he died.

Officials said at the time that a second trooper and a 40-year-old woman were hurt, neither by gunfire, and that a 35-year-old woman was checked for shortness of breath and declined a trip to the hospital.
## What Investigators Found

Rose is the gunman identified by police. Because he died that afternoon, he was never charged or tried, and what is known about him comes from the State Police investigation. He had previously lived in Connecticut and had been staying in the Wilmington area without a permanent address.

Detectives found no prior relationship, interaction or dispute between Rose and Snook. According to the State Police, Rose had told people who knew him that he believed police were targeting him, had recently posted anti-police content on social media, and had described himself as a victim of "gang stalking," which the release defines as a belief that someone is constantly surveilled and harassed by the government or law enforcement. Detectives concluded, as the Associated Press reported, that this was "a deliberate and targeted attack on law enforcement." They found no evidence that he acted for or with any group or other person.

The handgun had been bought legally by Rose in Connecticut in 2021. The State Police said he was not prohibited from buying or possessing guns, then or later, and had a limited criminal record. He had limited contact with Delaware police in the year before the shooting, and none of it was criminal in nature, led to an arrest or involved Snook.
## The Response

Gov. Matt Meyer called the shooting "an act of pure evil" and said that without the heroism of several troopers and other officers, "the consequences could have been so much worse." Col. William Crotty, the State Police superintendent, said: "His last actions were that of a hero – a hero who saved lives today."

On December 29, Lauren Snook and Snook's brother, Josh, spoke at a candlelight vigil in Hockessin. "He lived his life with integrity and heart, and that's how we choose to remember him here tonight," she said.

His funeral was held January 5, 2026, at the University of Delaware's Bob Carpenter Center in Newark, with thousands of mourners and officers from across the region. Burial was private. "He planned to come home, he planned a life, and when his life was taken, his legacy was not," his wife told the crowd. Meyer said there are Delawareans alive today "because Ty lived and because he served."
## What Has Happened Since
On January 13, U.S. Sens. Chris Coons and Lisa Blunt Rochester introduced a Senate resolution honoring Snook's life and bravery.

The DMV stayed closed for almost three months. It reopened March 10, 2026, with changes made on advice from police and employees. There is now a single entrance and exit, and every customer passes through a weapons detection system staffed by private security, which the state has put in at all of its DMV facilities. The greeter station was rebuilt as a glass-enclosed area with a trooper posted inside, and a separate room was added for watching video of the lobby. Appointments were required for the first month. Inside, a wall honors Snook with a collage of words his wife used in her eulogy.

On April 17, the National Law Enforcement Officers Memorial Fund announced that Snook's name would be engraved on the memorial in Washington, D.C., one of 363 officers added this year, with the names formally recognized at the 38th Annual Candlelight Vigil on the National Mall on May 13. In early May, Lauren Snook spoke at the 53rd annual Delaware Law Enforcement Officers Memorial Service on Legislative Mall in Dover.

The State Police's January release ends on Snook rather than on the man who shot him: "Ty's courageous act of strength and sacrifice reflected the core values he lived by every day—protecting others with bravery, selflessness, and steadfast integrity."

posts.title: The Menendez Brothers: Murders, Trials, Resentencing and Parole
posts.author: Cory
posts.excerpt: How the 1989 Beverly Hills killings led to two trials, a 1996 life sentence, a 2025 resentencing, a parole denial and a March 2027 hearing.
body: On August 18, 1989, Lyle and Erik Menendez bought two shotguns at a Big 5 Sporting Goods store in San Diego. Erik used a driver's license stolen from Donovan Goodreau, a friend of Lyle's. Two days later, their parents, José and Mary Louise "Kitty" Menendez, were shot to death in the family's Beverly Hills home.

The brothers were convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced in 1996 to life without parole. Nearly three decades later, a judge resentenced them, a parole board turned them down, and the board then moved their next hearing up to March 2027. Here is what the record shows, from the gun counter to the parole board.
## August 1989

Shotguns were not the first plan. That day the brothers visited several Southern California gun stores looking for handguns. A two-week waiting period and a problem with Lyle's driver's license pushed them to shotguns instead.

On the evening of August 20, José and Kitty were watching The Spy Who Loved Me in the den of the house. Lyle and Erik came in carrying the loaded shotguns. José was shot six times, including a fatal shot to the back of the head. Kitty was shot ten times. Lyle went back to the car, reloaded with ammunition Erik handed him, and fired the last shot.

Then they tried to build an alibi. They planned to buy tickets for Batman and dropped the idea when they realized the theater time-stamped its ticket stubs. They got rid of their bloodstained clothes, buried the shotguns along Mulholland Drive, and went to the Taste of L.A. festival at the Santa Monica Civic Auditorium. Back home, Lyle called 911 and told the operator, "Someone killed my parents!"
## The Money

Lyle suggested the killings were a mob hit tied to his father's business. José was the chief executive of Live Entertainment, and detectives looked at that angle first. What changed their focus was the spending. The brothers left the mansion empty and moved into adjoining condominiums in Marina del Rey.

Lyle bought Chuck's Spring Street Café, a Buffalo wing restaurant in Princeton, New Jersey, along with three Rolex watches and a Porsche Carrera. Erik hired a full-time tennis coach and played tournaments overseas. They traveled to the Caribbean and London. In all they spent about $700,000, most of it from a $650,000 life insurance policy.

Family members said the spending meant nothing and that the brothers' habits had not changed. Police also heard from Glenn Stevens, a friend of Lyle's. Stevens said that a week after the killings, Lyle made a sudden trip home from Princeton to destroy something on the family computer. A computer expert Lyle hired later said he had been paid to make sure a new will José had prepared was deleted.
## The Screenplay, the Therapist and the Arrests

Erik and a high school classmate, Craig Cignarelli, had written an amateur screenplay called Friends, about a wealthy young man who commits the "perfect murder" by killing his parents for their inheritance. Cignarelli went to police and said Erik had confessed to him. Police had him wear a wire to a lunch with Erik, but Erik did not confess on the recording.

Erik did confess to his psychologist, Jerome Oziel. Oziel told his mistress, Judalon Smyth, and began recording his sessions with both brothers. After the relationship ended badly, Smyth went to police and told them about the brothers and the tapes.

Lyle was arrested outside the Beverly Hills house on March 8, 1990. Erik turned himself in three days later, after flying back to Los Angeles from a tennis tournament in Israel. Both were held without bail. After two years of litigation over therapist-patient privilege, the Supreme Court of California ruled in August 1992 that most of the tapes could be used.
## The First Trial

The first trial began in July 1993 and was broadcast on Court TV. Leslie Abramson represented Erik and Jill Lansing represented Lyle. The defense said the brothers killed out of fear for their lives after years of sexual, emotional and physical abuse by José. Erik testified that he first told Lyle about the abuse about two weeks before the killings, and that the shotguns were bought for protection.

Prosecutor Pam Bozanich argued there was no imminent danger. She used the Oziel tapes, in which the brothers said they had planned the killings "beforehand," and pointed out that neither the tapes nor Erik's earlier statements to Cignarelli mentioned sexual abuse. She played Lyle's 911 call to show the jury how convincingly he could perform.

Two cousins testified for the defense. Diane Vander Molen said Lyle confided in her about abuse during a stay with the family in 1976. Andy Cano said Erik told him about it when they were children. Each brother had his own jury, and both deadlocked: female jurors leaned toward voluntary manslaughter, male jurors toward first-degree murder. The trial ended in a mistrial in January 1994.
## The Retrial and Conviction

Los Angeles County District Attorney Gil Garcetti retried the case in 1995. Judge Stanley Weisberg kept cameras out of the courtroom, citing the risk that jurors would be exposed to outside information, and limited the defense to 64 witnesses. Erik testified for fifteen days. Lyle did not testify.

Prosecutor David Conn asked Erik why he had not simply joined the Army to get away from his father. Conn introduced a letter Lyle allegedly wrote to an ex-girlfriend, Traci Baker, that included instructions on how to testify. Forensic psychiatrist Park Dietz testified that Erik did not show signs of "learned helplessness," noting that he had bought guns and practiced at a shooting range.

Weisberg found there was not enough evidence that the brothers were in imminent danger when they killed their parents. Both were convicted of two counts of first-degree murder with the special circumstance of lying in wait, plus conspiracy to commit murder. On July 2, 1996, they were sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
## The Habeas Petition and the Resentencing

State and federal courts rejected their appeals for years, starting in 1998. In May 2023, their lawyers filed a habeas corpus petition built on two new pieces of evidence: a 1988 letter that appears to have been written by Erik to Andy Cano describing abuse, and the account of former Menudo member Roy Rosselló, who said on NBC's Today in April 2023 that José Menendez drugged and raped him when he was 14.

On October 24, 2024, Los Angeles County District Attorney George Gascón asked the court to resentence the brothers, citing their time served, their conduct in prison and the dysfunction in the Menendez home. His successor, Nathan Hochman, reversed that position, opposed the habeas petition, and called the self-defense claims "self-serving lies."

On May 13, 2025, Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Michael Jesic resentenced both brothers to 50 years to life. Erik was 18 and Lyle 21 at the time of the killings, which put them under California's youth offender parole rules and made them eligible for parole immediately. Jesic said they had "done enough in the past 35 years that one day they should get that chance," and added, "I'm not suggesting they should be released."
## Where the Case Stands, October 2026

The California Board of Parole Hearings denied Erik parole on August 21, 2025, and Lyle the next day. Both denials were for three years. Commissioners cited repeated rule violations, especially contraband cellphones.
On September 16, 2025, Los Angeles Superior Court Judge William Ryan denied the habeas petition for a new trial. He wrote that neither piece of new evidence was "particularly strong."

Then, in early September 2026, the parole board granted both brothers an earlier parole suitability hearing, tentatively set for March 2027 instead of August 2028. The board relied on a provision of Proposition 9, a 2008 ballot measure, that lets a hearing be moved up when circumstances change or new information suggests a person may be suitable for parole.

Gov. Gavin Newsom also has the power to grant clemency, including a commutation. As of early October 2026 he had not done so, and both brothers remain in prison. The March 2027 hearing is the next scheduled decision in a case that began with a shotgun purchase 37 years ago.

posts.title: The Delphi Murders: Bridge Guy, Richard Allen and the Appeal
posts.author: Cory
posts.excerpt: Richard Allen was convicted in 2024 of killing Abby Williams and Libby German. The evidence, the trial, and where his appeal stands in October 2026.
body: Three days after Abby Williams and Libby German were killed near Delphi, Indiana, Richard Allen told investigators he had been on the trail that afternoon. The tip sheet listed him as "Richard Allen Whiteman," was marked cleared, and sat misfiled for more than five years. A volunteer clerk found it on September 21, 2022. Five weeks later, Allen was in custody.

A jury convicted Allen of both murders in November 2024, and he was sentenced to 130 years. His appeal was argued on September 21, 2026, and the Indiana Court of Appeals has not yet ruled. Here is the record, in order.
## The Disappearance on the Monon High Bridge

At 1:30 p.m. on February 13, 2017, 13-year-old Abigail "Abby" Williams and 14-year-old Liberty "Libby" German were dropped off by Libby's older sister, Kelsi German, on County Road 300 North, east of the Hoosier Heartland Highway. They planned to hike out to the Monon High Bridge over Deer Creek.

At 2:07 p.m., Libby posted a photo of Abby walking on the bridge to social media. Nobody heard from either girl after that. They did not meet Libby's father at 3:15 p.m. as planned, and they were reported missing at 5:30 p.m.
Around noon the next day, searchers found their bodies on the north bank of Deer Creek, about half a mile east of the bridge.
## What Libby's Phone Captured

Libby's phone held the most important evidence in the case. By February 15, 2017, Indiana State Police were circulating a still image from it of a man walking on the bridge toward the girls. He became known as "Bridge Guy." On February 22, police released audio from the same video, a man's voice saying, "Down the hill." They held back the rest to protect a future trial.

Investigators also found an unspent .40-caliber round within two feet of one of the bodies. At trial, state police digital examiner Christopher Cecil testified that the Bridge Guy video was recorded at 2:13 p.m. and that the phone's last recorded movement came at 2:32 p.m. The phone was found underneath Abby's body.
## The Misfiled Tip

Kathy Shank, a retired child protective services investigator, spent years as a volunteer organizing the thousands of tips that came in. On September 21, 2022, she found a tip sheet dated February 16, 2017. It said a "Richard Allen Whiteman" had been on the trails between 1:30 and 3:30 p.m. on the day of the murders and had seen three girls. It was marked clear.

Shank knew a Richard Allen lived on Whiteman Drive and concluded the street had been recorded as a surname. She took the file to Carroll County Sheriff Tony Liggett. Liggett later acknowledged that Allen, who came forward on his own and never left town, had "fell in the cracks."
Allen was taken into custody on October 26, 2022. On October 31, Indiana State Police announced he had been charged with two counts of murder. He pleaded not guilty.
## The Probable Cause Affidavit

Judge Frances Gull unsealed the probable cause affidavit on November 29, 2022. Investigators said they believed Allen was the man in the video. A lab had determined that the unspent round found near the bodies had been cycled through a Sig Sauer P226 pistol that Allen owned.

The affidavit also described witnesses. One said she saw a man walking away from the area "wearing a blue colored jacket and blue jeans and was muddy and bloody." Others saw a car parked behind a nearby building in a way that appeared to conceal its license plate. Investigators said it resembled the 2016 Ford Focus Allen owned.
When police interviewed Allen again in October 2022, he said he had gone to the bridge to watch the fish and had worn blue jeans and a blue or black Carhartt jacket that day.
## The Trial
The trial began on October 18, 2024, in Delphi. Prosecutors said both girls' throats were cut. Abby was found clothed in some of Libby's clothes; Libby was found nude.

Forensic pathologist Dr. Roland Kohr testified that both girls died of sharp force injuries to the neck and that he found no evidence of sexual assault. A state firearms examiner linked the unspent round to Allen's pistol. The defense called its own expert to dispute that comparison.

The core of the state's case was Allen's own words. Prosecutors said he admitted to the murders more than 60 times while jailed, to his wife, his mother, other family members, the prison warden, a prison psychologist and other inmates. Master Trooper Brian Harshman, who reviewed more than 700 of Allen's recorded prison calls, testified that the voice saying "Down the hill" was Allen's. In an April 2023 call played for the jury, Allen told his wife, "I did it. I killed Abby and Libby." She answered that he had not and that he was not feeling well.

Prison psychologist Monica Wala testified about what Allen told her. According to her clinical notes, he described following the girls across the bridge, ordering them down a hill and across the creek, wanting to sexually assault them, and instead cutting their throats and covering their bodies with branches. She diagnosed him with a brief psychotic disorder in May 2023.
## The Defense and the Verdict

The defense argued that the confessions were not reliable. Allen had spent 13 months in solitary confinement before trial, and his lawyers said his mental health collapsed there and that he was psychotic when he made the statements. Defense witnesses described his deterioration in custody.

On November 11, 2024, the jury convicted Allen on all counts. On December 20, 2024, Judge Gull sentenced him to 65 years for the murder of Libby and 65 years for the murder of Abby, to be served consecutively, for a total of 130 years.
## Where It Stands, October 2026

On April 9, 2025, the interrogation and prison confession videos shown at trial were released to the public. On July 18, 2025, Indiana moved Allen out of state, to the Lexington Assessment and Reception Center in Oklahoma, where he remains while the appeal is pending.

His appellate brief, filed in December 2025, raises three main issues. First, that the detective who got the search warrant for his home mischaracterized witness descriptions to tie him to Bridge Guy. Second, that his confessions should have been excluded because they came out of solitary confinement, suicide watch and psychosis. Third, that he could not present a complete defense, because the judge kept out evidence pointing to other people and expert testimony about his confessions. The Indiana Attorney General's office has asked the court to uphold the convictions.

A three-judge panel, Nancy Vaidik, Robert Altice and Elaine Brown, heard oral argument in Indianapolis on September 21, 2026. Deputy Attorney General Ellen Meilaender told the court the restrictive housing was for Allen's protection and that the timeline, the eyewitness evidence and his own statements proved he was Bridge Guy. One judge pushed back on that, telling the state, "You protected him into psychosis." The court will issue a written decision, which could take months. Until it does, the convictions and the 130-year sentence stand.
In Delphi, the L & A Park Foundation was formed to build a park in the girls' memory, and Delphi Community Middle School, which both attended, renamed its library the Abby and Libby Memorial Library.

posts.title: Genetic Genealogy Cases: What It Has Solved and What It Cannot Do
posts.author: Cory
posts.excerpt: From Angie Dodge to the Boy in the Box: cases genetic genealogy solved, the wrong turns along the way, and the limits courts and families still face.
body: In June 1996, Brian Leigh Dripps Sr. lived in Idaho Falls, Idaho, across the street from the home of 18-year-old Angie Dodge. Police interviewed him in a neighborhood canvass five days after she was raped and killed in her apartment. Then the case went another direction for more than two decades, and an innocent man went to prison. What finally brought detectives back across that street was a family tree built from strangers' DNA.

That technique is investigative genetic genealogy. A separate post on this site explains how it works and the rules that govern it. This one is about results: what it has solved, and where it has gone wrong or simply run out of road.

The best public count comes from criminologist Tracey Dowdeswell's Forensic Genetic Genealogy Project. Through the end of 2023, it recorded 651 criminal cases solved with the method, counted as victim-offender pairs, involving 318 identified perpetrators. Separately, it recorded 461 unidentified people given back their names, plus three disaster victims. The count starts in 2015, three years before the Golden State Killer arrest made the method famous.
## Angie Dodge: a false confession and a false lead

In January 1997, Idaho Falls police questioned Christopher Tapp, then 20. After more than 100 hours of interrogation he confessed, though no physical evidence tied him to the scene and his accounts contradicted one another. In May 1998 he was convicted of aiding and abetting Dodge's rape and murder and sentenced to a minimum of 30 years. He recanted in 2001.

The DNA at the scene was not his, and police kept looking for its source. In 2014 they obtained a court order to search a Y-chromosome genealogy database that Ancestry.com had acquired from the Sorenson Molecular Genealogy Foundation. A sample there, given years earlier by a man named Michael Usry Sr., matched the crime scene profile at 34 of 35 markers. That pointed police to his son, Michael Usry Jr., a filmmaker in New Orleans. Investigators questioned him and took a saliva sample. It did not match, and he was never charged. Usry called the investigation a serious breach of his and his father's privacy.
## The tree that found Dripps

In late 2018, Idaho Falls police brought in genetic genealogist CeCe Moore of Parabon NanoLabs, who searched GEDmatch for relatives of the unknown man. The matches led to one couple, Clarence and Cleo Ussery, whose descendants had to include the person who left the DNA. Moore identified six known male descendants. One had lived in Idaho in 1996. Police followed him and collected his DNA, and it did not match.

After about three more months of research, Moore found a seventh descendant the first round had missed: Brian Leigh Dripps Sr. Police collected a cigarette butt he threw from his car window. The DNA matched. Dripps was arrested in May 2019 and confessed. In February 2021 he pleaded guilty to first-degree rape and murder, and in June 2021 a judge sentenced him to 20 years to life.

Tapp's rape conviction had been vacated in 2017 and he was released. He was fully exonerated of the murder in July 2019. In June 2022 the city of Idaho Falls settled his lawsuit for $11.7 million, and the mayor apologized. Tapp died on November 5, 2023, at 47, after a fall in Las Vegas.
## Serial cases

The method has named offenders behind long series of attacks. Roy Charles Waller, called the NorCal Rapist, assaulted nine women in Northern California between 1991 and 2006. Crime scene DNA was matched through GEDmatch to one of his relatives, and he was arrested in September 2018. A jury convicted him on 46 counts in November 2020, and he was sentenced to 897 years to life.

In Shelby County, Indiana, a series of violent home invasions and sexual assaults between 1982 and 1985 went unsolved for decades. Parabon's genealogy work narrowed the suspects to Steven Ray Hessler or his brother, and investigators confirmed the lead with DNA from an envelope Hessler had sealed to pay a utility bill. A jury convicted him on all counts in March 2022, and he was sentenced to 650 years.

In Fort Wayne, Indiana, eight-year-old April Tinsley disappeared on April 1, 1988, after going back for her umbrella. A jogger found her body in a ditch near Spencerville three days later. For years afterward, the man who killed her left notes taunting police, including a message written on a barn in 1990 and notes left on girls' bicycles in 2004. In May 2018 a Fort Wayne detective sent the DNA to Parabon. By July 2, Moore had narrowed it to two brothers. Detectives found DNA in John D. Miller's trash that matched, and when they approached him on July 15, 2018, he said April Tinsley's name before they did. Miller pleaded guilty that December and was sentenced to 80 years. He died in a hospital on September 4, 2025, at 66.
## Names for the dead

Hundreds of the method's results are identifications, not arrests. In February 1957 a boy was found beaten to death in a cardboard box in Philadelphia's Fox Chase neighborhood. For 65 years he was the Boy in the Box. In December 2022 Philadelphia police announced that DNA and genetic genealogy had identified him as Joseph Augustus Zarelli, who was 4. Both of his parents are dead, and the homicide investigation remains open.

In Allenstown, New Hampshire, a barrel holding the remains of a woman and a girl was found near Bear Brook State Park in 1985, and a second barrel holding two more girls was found nearby in 2000. Genealogy work identified the man the state attorney general's office holds responsible, Terry Peder Rasmussen, in 2017; he had died in prison in 2010 while serving a sentence for a different killing. Three victims were named in 2019: Marlyse Honeychurch and her daughters Marie Vaughn and Sarah McWaters. In September 2025 the DNA Doe Project and New Hampshire State Police identified the fourth as Rea Rasmussen, his daughter, about 3 years old. Her mother, Pepper Reed, has not been seen since the late 1970s.

On April 11, 1975, a fisherman found the body of a teenage girl in the Mississippi River in Clinton County, Iowa. She had been shot in the head and was about 10 weeks pregnant. In October 2025, 16 volunteer genealogists from the DNA Doe Project worked her case over a weekend. In June 2026 the project announced her name: Cheryl Lynn Edwards, 15, of Waukegan, Illinois. The sheriff's office says it can now investigate her killing.

In November 2000 the dismembered body of a teenage girl was found on the grounds of the Soldiers' Home in Chelsea, Massachusetts. Eugene McCollom is serving a life sentence for her murder, yet for 26 years no one knew her name. On June 3, 2026, prosecutors announced that FBI investigators had used genetic genealogy to find her brother, and DNA confirmed she was Tiffany Bradley, 16, of Allentown, Pennsylvania.
## What it cannot do

It cannot find anyone whose relatives have not opted in. Since May 2019, GEDmatch has shown police only users who chose to allow it. If no cousins from your family have uploaded, there is no tree to build.

It produces a lead, not proof. Every case above ended with a conventional DNA comparison on a sample from the actual person. The Dodge case shows why. The first tree was right about the family and wrong about the man for months, and an earlier Y-chromosome search put an innocent filmmaker under suspicion for something he had nothing to do with.
It cannot put the dead on trial. Zarelli's parents and Rasmussen were gone before anyone had names. An identification answers who, but no court ever tests it.

Its methods can be challenged in court. Matthew Nilo, a lawyer, was arrested in May 2023 and charged with sexually assaulting women in Boston's Charlestown and North End neighborhoods in 2007 and 2008. He has pleaded not guilty. Investigators say genetic genealogy led them to him, and FBI agents then collected items he had used at a Manhattan restaurant in 2023. His lawyers argue the DNA was taken without a warrant. They also say the FBI searched MyHeritage, which they contend federal policy bars, and at a 2025 hearing prosecutors acknowledged the FBI had not documented what it found there. As of a June 2026 hearing in Suffolk Superior Court, the judge had not ruled on the motion to suppress, and no trial date had been reported.

Taken together, the record is strong. Hundreds of offenders named, hundreds of people buried under their own names again, and at least one wrongly convicted man cleared by the same tree that found the real killer. It is also a record of tools that work only when strangers have shared their DNA, that still depend on old-fashioned confirmation, and whose rules are still being argued in courtrooms.

posts.title: Why the JonBenét Ramsey Case Is Still Open After Nearly 30 Years
posts.author: Cory
posts.excerpt: Unknown DNA, a grand jury vote that never became a charge, and what Boulder police say they are doing now in the JonBenét Ramsey case.
body: The Boulder police file on JonBenét Ramsey holds nearly 2,500 pieces of evidence and about 40,000 reports, more than a million pages in all. Detectives have collected samples from more than 200 people. Nearly 30 years after the six-year-old was found dead in the basement of her family's home on December 26, 1996, no one has been charged.

The crime itself and the first decade of the investigation are covered in a separate post. This one is about why the case has not closed: a DNA profile that has never been matched to anyone, a grand jury vote that never became a prosecution, and what Boulder police say they are doing now.
## The Unknown DNA

Early in the investigation, analysts found male DNA in a drop of blood on JonBenét's underwear. It did not come from anyone in her family. In 2003 a profile from that sample was entered into CODIS, the FBI's national DNA database. It has never produced a match.

In 2008, the office of Boulder County District Attorney Mary Lacy sent JonBenét's long underwear to Bode Technology, a private lab near Washington, D.C., for "touch DNA" testing, which looks for skin cells left by contact. The lab found previously undetected male genetic material on the sides of the garment, where an attacker would have grasped it, and it was consistent with the profile from the underwear.

On July 9, 2008, Lacy announced that the Ramsey family was no longer under suspicion. In a letter to John Ramsey she wrote: "To the extent that we may have contributed in any way to the public perception that you might have been involved in this crime, I am deeply sorry." Patsy Ramsey had died of cancer two years earlier.

The letter has been disputed since. In 2016 Lacy's successor, Stan Garnett, said: "This letter is not legally binding. It's a good-faith opinion and has no legal importance." The same year the Boulder Daily Camera reported that independent DNA experts who reviewed the lab data believed the profile might be a composite of more than one person, which would limit its value for identifying anyone. Former police chief Mark Beckner, who did not agree with the exoneration, has said the unknown DNA should still be the focus of the investigation.

The sample is also small. In November 2022 Boulder police said the DNA available is "extremely small and complex" and that the sample "could, in whole or in part, be consumed by DNA testing." A test that uses up the evidence cannot be run again. The department has said that whenever a proven technology can reliably test samples like these, more analysis will be done, and that it has discussed genetic genealogy with private labs alongside the Colorado Bureau of Investigation and the FBI.
## The Grand Jury

A Boulder County grand jury began hearing evidence on September 15, 1998, and sat for 13 months. On October 13, 1999, District Attorney Alex Hunter announced there would be no charges. "I and my prosecutorial team believe we do not have sufficient evidence to warrant the filing of charges against anyone who has been investigated at this time," he said.

He did not disclose that the jurors had voted to indict. The Boulder Daily Camera reported the vote earlier in 2013, and on October 25, 2013, after its reporter went to court, a judge released the four pages signed by the grand jury foreman. They listed two counts against each parent. The first, child abuse resulting in death, alleged that John and Patsy Ramsey permitted JonBenét to be "unreasonably placed in a situation which posed a threat of injury to the child's life or health." The second, accessory to a crime, alleged that each had helped a person suspected of first-degree murder and child abuse resulting in death. The pages did not identify that person. Because Hunter never signed the indictment, no charge was filed.

A grand jury indictment requires only probable cause. A conviction requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt. Garnett said in 2013 that the documents meant the jurors found probable cause on the evidence they heard, that when he had the proposed charges reviewed he "was told that they related to charges for which the statute of limitations had run years ago," and that "everyone, including the Ramsey family, is entitled to the full presumption of innocence." The family's lawyer, L. Lin Wood, called the released pages "a mere snippet of the case" that did not account for the 2008 DNA testing.
## Burke Ramsey

JonBenét's brother, Burke, was nine. In 1999 both the police and the district attorney's office said publicly that he was not a suspect. A 2016 CBS documentary series nonetheless put forward the theory that he had killed his sister. He sued CBS and others for defamation, seeking $750 million, and on January 4, 2019, his lawyer said the case had "been amicably settled to the satisfaction of all parties."
## Where the Case Stands, October 2026

Boulder police took the case back from the district attorney in February 2009 and have treated it as an open homicide since. Detectives have followed up on more than 21,000 tips, letters and emails and traveled to 19 states to interview or speak with more than 1,000 people. In 2023 the Colorado Cold Case Review Team spent a year building a searchable database of the file. Its recommendations have not been made public.

Stephen Redfearn, named police chief in September 2024, issues an update near each anniversary. On December 12, 2025, he said: "This past year, our detectives have conducted several new interviews as well as re-interviewed individuals based on tips we've received. We have also collected new evidence and tested and re-tested other pieces of evidence to generate new leads." The department has not said what the new evidence is or who was interviewed.

John Ramsey has pressed police since at least 2024 to send evidence to a private lab for forensic genetic genealogy, the method that has identified suspects in other cold cases by tracing a DNA profile through relatives. In June 2026 Yvonne "Missy" Woods, a former Colorado Bureau of Investigation DNA analyst, pleaded guilty to four felonies tied to her lab work, which raised new questions about the case. Boulder police said a CBI review of the records found Woods's conduct had no effect on the Ramsey investigation, and the district attorney's office said the same.

The department's position is that nothing is being left untested. Its case page says: "The assertion that there is viable evidence and leads we are not pursuing—to include DNA testing—is completely false."

December 26, 2026, will be 30 years. As of early October 2026, no arrest has been made and no one has been charged. Boulder police ask anyone with information to call 303-441-1974 or email BouldersMostWanted@bouldercolorado.gov.

posts.title: The Watts Family Murders: The Weeks Before and the Evidence After
posts.author: Cory
posts.excerpt: Chris Watts pleaded guilty in 2018 to killing his pregnant wife and two daughters. What the released case file shows about the weeks before and after.
body: On August 14, 2018, the day after Shanann Watts and her daughters were reported missing, her mother called police in Frederick, Colorado. According to a police report later released by prosecutors, Sandra Rzucek said her son-in-law was acting "weird" and out of the ordinary, and that she suspected foul play.

The next night he was under arrest. Christopher Lee Watts later pleaded guilty to murdering Shanann, 34, who was 15 weeks pregnant with a son the family planned to name Nico, and their daughters Bella, 4, and Celeste, 3. This post sets out the timeline from the court record and from the nearly 2,000 pages the Weld County District Attorney's Office released after sentencing, including what those pages show about the weeks before.
## The Weeks Before

Shanann worked from home selling a nutritional product called Thrive for the multi-level marketing company Le-Vel. Chris was an operator for Anadarko Petroleum. The couple bought their five-bedroom house at 2825 Saratoga Trail in Frederick in 2013 and filed for bankruptcy in 2015.

At the end of June 2018, Shanann took the girls to North Carolina for an extended family visit. Chris joined them for the last week. By then he was seeing Nichol Kessinger, who worked for an Anadarko contractor. Kessinger later told The Denver Post that he said he was separated and nearly finished with a divorce, that they saw each other four to five times a week from early July, and that he called from North Carolina to say the divorce was final. He had never filed for divorce.

The released records show what Shanann was living with. In texts to friends she described her husband as cold and distant, said he had rebuffed her affection and would not hold her hand during an ultrasound, and worried about having a third child with a man who seemed uninterested. On August 5 she texted him: "You don't fall out of love in 5 weeks." A few days later she told a friend that Chris had said he was "scared to death about this third baby." When the friend raised the possibility of another woman, Shanann said she had asked him and he had denied it.

He was also lying about where he was. On Saturday, August 11, while Shanann was on a work trip to Arizona, he left the girls with a babysitter and told people, police among them, that he had gone to a Colorado Rockies game and then to dinner with friends. Kessinger told police she was the one who had dinner with him that night.

Read together, after the fact, those records show a marriage under strain and a husband hiding an affair from his wife and lying to the woman he was seeing. At the time they were visible in pieces to different people, and only some of them to Shanann. They do not explain what he did, and his own explanations have changed more than once.
## August 13

Shanann got home from Arizona at about 1:48 a.m. on Monday, August 13. Her friend and colleague Nickole Utoft Atkinson dropped her off. Later that morning Shanann missed an obstetrics appointment and stopped answering texts. Atkinson went to the house at about 12:10 p.m., got no answer, contacted Chris at work and called Frederick police. An officer arrived for a welfare check at about 1:40 p.m., and Watts left work to let police into the house.

Inside were Shanann's purse, wallet, keys and medication. Her phone was later found between the couch cushions. Her car, with the girls' car seats in it, was in the garage, and her wedding ring was on a bedside table.

Watts told police that he and Shanann had an emotional but civil conversation about separating that morning. That afternoon he texted Kessinger that his family was "gone" and that Shanann had taken the girls to a play date. A neighbor's security camera had recorded Watts loading his work truck before dawn. When the neighbor played the footage for police with Watts in the room, he said he had been loading tools for work. The next day he stood outside the house and told a Denver television station, "I just want them back."
## The Confession and the Recovery

The FBI and the Colorado Bureau of Investigation joined the case on August 14. On the morning of August 15, Kessinger called the Weld County Sheriff's Office to tell investigators about the affair, and met with FBI agents that day. Watts took a polygraph examination and failed it. After talking with his father, Ronnie, he told investigators that he had strangled Shanann in a rage after seeing her on a baby monitor strangling Celeste, with Bella "sprawled" and blue on her bed. District Attorney Michael Rourke later called that account "a flat-out lie," and Watts's guilty plea admitted all three murders.

He was arrested that night. He told investigators where he had taken his family: an Anadarko oil site in rural Weld County. Before his confession, a police drone had already spotted a bedsheet in a field near the tanks that matched sheets found in the trash at the house. Shanann was found the next day in a shallow grave. Bella and Celeste were found inside oil tanks nearby. Anadarko fired him the day he was arrested.
## The Charges, the Plea and the Sentence

On August 20, Rourke charged Watts with nine felonies: five counts of first-degree murder, including two for the deaths of children under 12, one count of unlawful termination of a pregnancy, and three counts of tampering with a deceased human body.

On November 6, 2018, Watts pleaded guilty to all nine counts. Rourke had traveled to North Carolina to discuss a possible deal with Shanann's parents and brother after the defense approached him, and he said the family's wishes were the most compelling factor in not seeking the death penalty. He quoted Shanann's mother: "He made the choice to take their lives. I didn't want to be in the position to make the choice to take his."

On November 19, 2018, District Judge Marcelo Kopcow sentenced Watts to five life terms without the possibility of parole, three of them to run consecutively, plus 48 years for the unlawful termination of a pregnancy and 36 years for tampering with the bodies. In December 2018 he was moved out of Colorado for safety reasons to Dodge Correctional Institution in Waupun, Wisconsin, where he remains.
## His Later Accounts

On February 18, 2019, a CBI agent, an FBI agent and a Frederick detective interviewed Watts at the Wisconsin prison. In that account he said he strangled Shanann at home, then drove the girls, still alive, to the oil site and killed them there. He said the affair had contributed. In 2021 a pen pal, Cheryln Cadle, told Inside Edition that he had written to her that he planned the killings for weeks. Those letters are his own claims, relayed by a third party, and have not been tested in court.
## After

In November 2019 a Weld County judge ordered Watts to pay Shanann's parents, Frank and Sandy Rzucek, $6 million in a wrongful death suit he did not contest. The family filed it to keep him from profiting from the killings, not expecting to collect.

The family has also faced years of online harassment from people pushing theories about the case. In 2025 Shanann's brother, Frankie Rzucek, won a harassment and defamation case in the United Kingdom against a YouTuber, and the court ordered the channel shut down. "I never saw so much evil in this world," Frank Rzucek said in a 2026 Fox Nation special. "Towards us, towards other victims."

Shanann, Bella, Celeste and Nico are the people this case is about. What happened to them is settled by a guilty plea. Why it happened rests mostly on accounts from the man who lied to everyone around him, and those accounts have changed.
