posts.title: Courtney Clenney: The Killing of Christian Obumseli and the Plea
posts.author: Cory
posts.excerpt: Courtney Clenney pleaded guilty to manslaughter in the 2022 death of Christian Obumseli in Miami and was sentenced to six years. Here is the record.
body: At 4:57 p.m. on April 3, 2022, Courtney Clenney called 911 from the Miami apartment she shared with her boyfriend, Christian Obumseli, to report that he had been stabbed. According to prosecutors, Obumseli can be heard on the call saying he was dying and losing feeling in his arm, and Clenney can be heard saying, "I'm so sorry."

She later told police that Obumseli had attacked her and that she grabbed a knife and threw it at him from about 10 feet away. The medical examiner disagreed. The autopsy found that Obumseli died from a forceful downward thrust of a blade that went three inches into his chest and severed his subclavian artery, and concluded the wound could not have come from a knife thrown from that distance.

Obumseli was 27 and worked in cryptocurrency. Clenney, then 26, was a social media and OnlyFans model known online as Courtney Tailor. She was charged with second-degree murder and said she acted in self-defense. On August 10, 2026, after more than four years and several trial dates, she pleaded guilty to manslaughter with a deadly weapon and was sentenced to six years in prison.
## The Relationship Before Miami

The couple's relationship began in November 2020. Before Miami, they lived in a penthouse at the Berkshire Riverview in South Austin, Texas. A neighbor who lived below them told FOX 7 Austin that their fights were frequent and at times spilled into his space; during one, a tiger painting was thrown onto his tenth-floor balcony. He said police were called to the couple's apartment multiple times.

When Clenney was arrested, Miami-Dade State Attorney Katherine Fernandez Rundle called the relationship "tempestuous and combative" and said the violence continued after the move to Miami, to the point that their building was prepared to evict them. Two videos from February 2022 were reported: one from a trip to Aspen, Colorado, that appears to show Clenney yelling at and repeatedly hitting Obumseli, and a building elevator video that appeared to show her shoving and hitting him.
## The Arrest and the Self-Defense Claim

Clenney was arrested in August 2022, four months after Obumseli's death, at a rehabilitation facility in Hawaii where her attorney said she was being treated for substance abuse and post-traumatic stress disorder. She was returned to Florida, pleaded not guilty, and was held without bond for the rest of the case.

Her attorney, Frank Prieto, argued the stabbing was self-defense and pushed for the case to be treated as manslaughter rather than murder. The defense said Obumseli had engaged in a pattern of physical violence, intimidation and emotional abuse, and prepared to argue that Clenney was a battered partner. Obumseli's family has maintained that he was the victim of domestic violence.

A defense filing laid out text messages the lawyers planned to use. In an April 2021 exchange, Clenney accused Obumseli of hitting her in the face; he allegedly replied that he was trying to move her hand and did not mean to hit her. In August 2021, she texted that he had been punching her in the back.

The filing described other alleged incidents: a dislocated shoulder during a September 2021 argument about leaving a pool, fractured ribs during a 2021 trip to Dubai after an argument about smoking marijuana, and an injured finger in Austin in January 2022. These were the defense's allegations. Because the case ended in a plea, a jury never weighed them.
## The Laptop Case

A separate case opened against Clenney's parents, Dewayne "Kim" and Deborah Clenney of Bee Cave, Texas. According to arrest affidavits, investigators believed Clenney gave Obumseli's laptop to her parents at some point between the killing and her arrest. The attorney for Obumseli's estate told investigators no one had been given permission to keep or access it.

The parents and Clenney herself were each charged with one count of unauthorized access to a computer, a third-degree felony in Florida. Search warrants for iCloud accounts turned up a group chat between the parents and Clenney's attorneys. In one message, her father allegedly wrote, "Hell yeah! That PIN worked." An attorney replied, "Kim. Hold off going through the computer please. I don't want to turn you into a witness just yet if you find something useful." Deborah Clenney allegedly took the laptop to an attorney in Dallas, and it was later turned over to an IT expert in Florida.

In July 2024, prosecutors dropped the computer charges against Clenney and her parents after a circuit judge ruled that the Miami-Dade State Attorney's Office had violated attorney-client privilege when investigators seized messages between the family and its lawyers. Jude Faccidomo, who represented the parents, called for the office to recuse itself from the murder case.
## The Civil Suit and the Delays

Obumseli's estate filed a civil lawsuit against Clenney and several companies connected to the apartment building. It accused Clenney of battery and alleged that the condominium, property management and security defendants failed to provide adequate security.

Clenney settled her part of that case before the criminal case ended. On December 3, 2025, the estate filed a notice of settlement as to Clenney only, and the claims against her were dismissed with prejudice on March 4, 2026. The terms are not public.

The criminal trial kept slipping. In December 2025, a judge denied Clenney bond again and set trial for April 27, 2026. That date did not hold: in late April, with prosecutors still needing to complete more than a dozen depositions, both sides jointly asked for more time. Circuit Judge Andrea Ricker Wolfson granted it and warned, "This really has to be a final continuance." Trial was reset for August 2026.
## The Plea

On July 31, 2026, Prieto confirmed that Clenney had reached a deal, without disclosing its terms. On August 10, 2026, in a Miami courtroom, she pleaded guilty to manslaughter with a deadly weapon, reduced from second-degree murder.

She was sentenced to six years in prison followed by five years of probation, with credit for the nearly four years she had already spent in custody. That means she could be released and begin probation in about two years. After release she must undergo mental health and substance abuse evaluations and treatment.

Prosecutors said she should not be allowed to profit from the killing and that they would support any effort by the Florida Attorney General's Office to stop her. "We do believe that nobody should benefit financially from murdering somebody," Assistant State Attorney Shawn Abuhoff said. Rundle said in a statement that Obumseli's family "finally heard what they long sought: Courtney Clenney accepting full responsibility for his death."
## The Family in Court

Obumseli's family told the court he was someone who loved deeply and had stayed in a destructive relationship despite earlier violence. They said he had written about fears that his love for Clenney could cost him his life. "Your actions have left the Obumseli family with a void that can never be filled," a family representative said.

His mother, Chio Obumseli, described him as kindhearted, compassionate, friendly and respectful. "Four years later, there are still nights when I cannot sleep," she said. "Nothing can describe what it feels like for a mother to stand at the grave of her child." She told the court the day closed a legal chapter but not the family's grief.

A plea ends a case without a trial, so the competing accounts of the relationship were never tested before a jury. What the record settles is the conviction: Courtney Clenney pleaded guilty to manslaughter with a deadly weapon in the death of Christian Obumseli.

posts.title: How Investigators Tied Bryan Kohberger to the Moscow Murders
posts.author: Cory
posts.excerpt: A car on camera, a phone that went quiet for two hours and DNA on a knife sheath: how investigators tied Bryan Kohberger to the Moscow killings.
body: The first thread was a car. Cameras around 1122 King Road in Moscow, Idaho, recorded a white Hyundai Elantra passing the house several times in the early hours of November 13, 2022, then leaving the area at 4:20 a.m. Within seven weeks, investigators had tied that kind of car, a phone that went quiet for two hours and DNA on a knife sheath to one man: Bryan Christopher Kohberger, a 28-year-old criminology doctoral student at Washington State University. He pleaded guilty in 2025. This post follows how the case against him was built.

Four University of Idaho students were killed that night. Madison Mogen, 21, was a senior studying marketing. Kaylee Goncalves, 21, was a senior in general studies. Xana Kernodle, 20, was a junior studying marketing. Ethan Chapin, 20, was a freshman in recreation, sport and tourism management and a member of Sigma Chi. In May 2023 the university awarded posthumous degrees to Mogen and Goncalves and certificates to Kernodle and Chapin.
## The House on King Road

Five women rented the three-story house at 1122 King Road for the fall 2022 semester. Mogen and Goncalves had rooms on the third floor. Kernodle and Dylan Mortensen lived on the second floor, and Bethany Funke lived on the first. Chapin, Kernodle's boyfriend, was staying over.

According to the probable cause affidavit, Chapin and Kernodle came home from a party at the Sigma Chi house around 1:45 a.m. Mogen and Goncalves got back at about 1:56 a.m. after a night out downtown. Kernodle was still awake after 4 a.m. She received a DoorDash delivery around then, and her phone showed her on TikTok minutes later.
## What the Surviving Roommate Described

Mortensen told police she was woken by sounds she first took for Goncalves playing with her dog upstairs. She heard someone she believed was Goncalves say something to the effect of "there's someone here." The affidavit notes that the voice may have been Kernodle's. Later she heard crying and a male voice say something like "it's ok, I'm going to help you." At 4:17 a.m., a nearby security camera picked up what the affidavit called "distorted audio of what sounded like voices or a whimper followed by a loud thud."

When Mortensen opened her door again, she saw a figure in black clothing, with a mask covering the mouth and nose, walk toward the sliding glass back door. She described a man at least 5 feet 10 inches tall, "not very muscular, but athletically built with bushy eyebrows." She said she stood in a "frozen shock phase" and then locked herself in her room. Between 4:22 and 4:24 a.m., she and Funke traded worried texts.

No one called police that night. A 911 call from one of the surviving roommates' phones came in just before noon to report an unconscious person, and officers found all four victims dead. Autopsy reports released by the City of Moscow in July 2025 found that all four died of stab wounds from a single-edged, non-serrated knife. Kernodle had more than 50 wounds, many of them defensive.
## The Car and the Phone

Investigators collected video from around the neighborhood and followed a white Elantra making repeated passes, the first at about 3:29 a.m. and another at 4:04 a.m., before it left at 4:20. An FBI examiner first identified it as a 2011 to 2013 model, then said it could be as late as 2016. On November 29, a Washington State University police officer looking for white Elantras found a 2015 model registered to Kohberger, who lived in Pullman, just across the state line. Another officer learned he had switched the car's registration from Pennsylvania to Washington on November 18, five days after the killings.

Phone records added more. The affidavit says Kohberger's phone moved south from Pullman at about 2:47 a.m. and then stopped reporting to the network until 4:48 a.m., when it reappeared south of Moscow. Investigators wrote that this was consistent with an attempt to conceal his location. The same phone was back near King Road around 9 a.m., hours before the 911 call. Records also put it near the house at least 12 times before the murders, nearly always late at night or early in the morning.
## The Sheath and the Family Tree

The central physical evidence was a tan leather Ka-Bar knife sheath, stamped with a USMC insignia, found on the bed next to Mogen's body. Analysts recovered a single male DNA profile from the sheath's button snap. It matched no one in the national law enforcement database.

Investigators turned to investigative genetic genealogy, which compares crime-scene DNA with people who have uploaded their own DNA to consumer services. On November 22, the sample went to the private lab Othram. The New York Times reported that Othram's closest match shared just 70.7 centimorgans with the sample, a distant relationship. On December 10 the FBI took over the genealogy work and found a match of 250 centimorgans somewhere in the family tree, a much stronger lead. The Times also reported that the FBI's searches reached consumer DNA data that is restricted for law enforcement use, including MyHeritage.

A family tree is a lead, not proof. In December, Kohberger and his father drove the Elantra across the country to his parents' house in Albrightsville, Pennsylvania. On December 15 the car was stopped twice in Indiana for following too closely. Agents then watched him in Pennsylvania. A law enforcement source told CNN that he was seen outside the house wearing surgical gloves, that he cleaned his car "inside and outside, not missing an inch," and that around 4 a.m. one morning he put trash bags in a neighbor's bins.
On December 27, investigators collected trash from the family home. According to the affidavit, DNA from it came from the biological father of the man whose DNA was on the sheath.
## The Arrest

Pennsylvania State Police and the FBI arrested Kohberger at the house on December 30, 2022. Michael Mancuso, a Monroe County, Pennsylvania, prosecutor, later said Kohberger was found in the kitchen wearing latex gloves and putting his trash into separate Ziploc bags. Warrant records unsealed in March 2023 list what was seized from the home, including a Glock pistol, a Smith & Wesson pocketknife and black face masks. Kohberger waived extradition and was flown to Idaho on January 4, 2023.
## Testing the Evidence

The defense went after the genetic genealogy, arguing that the way the FBI built the family tree violated his rights. In February 2025, Judge Steven Hippler refused to suppress the DNA and data from Kohberger's online accounts, writing that "suppression is not warranted on any of these issues."

None of it reached a jury. Kohberger was indicted in May 2023 on four counts of first-degree murder and one count of felony burglary, and prosecutors sought the death penalty. On July 2, 2025, he pleaded guilty to all five counts under a deal that took death off the table, and on July 23 he was sentenced to four consecutive life terms without parole plus 10 years. In July 2026 he petitioned to withdraw the plea, saying he is innocent and was pressured by his former lawyers. The legal history, from the venue change to the plea and the challenge now pending, is in our companion post, Murders in Moscow: The Kohberger Plea and the Fight to Undo It.

The house on King Road was demolished on December 28, 2023. On August 21, 2024, the University of Idaho dedicated the Vandal Healing Garden and Memorial on its Moscow campus in honor of the four students. A motive has never been established. Offered the chance to speak at his sentencing, Kohberger declined.
